EUGENE S. HOPP

EUGENE S. HOPP
Grand Mas ter
October 13, 1967 -October 18. 1968

Grand Master October 13, 1967-0ctober 18, 1968
Eugene S. ("Gene") Hopp, our 102d Grand Master, is the seventh
physician and surgeon to serve as Grand Master and the first since 1903.
Born in New York City on April 25, 1910. He received his B.S.
degree from the University of Georgia in 1933. A member of Phi Beta
Kappa and Phi Kappa Phi, honor scholas tic societies, he also was captain
of the swimming team and winner of cups for public speaking.
Dr. Hopp received his M .D . degree from the University of Georgia
School of Medicine in 1937, served a year of internship in Los Angeles,
and then a year and a half of surgery a t Vancouver Barracks Hospital.
He was on active duty in the Medical Corps of the U.S. Army at Letter...
man Hospital. San Francisco, for four years in the specialty of ear, nose
and throat. Commencing in 1944, he served overseas for two years as
Chief of the Eye. Ear, Nose and Throat service of the 8lst General Hospital, European Theater, and was later appointed civilian consultant in
his specialty to the Surgeon General of the U.S. Army, and later to the
Surgeon General of the U .S. A ir Force. He was discharged from the
military as Lt. Colonel of the Medical Corps in July, 1946.
While at Vancouver Barracks Hospital, he met Isabell Armstrong,
of Lewiston, Idaho. and they were married in Seattle on April 3, 1940.
Their son, Michael Eugene, was born in San Francisco, on August 12,
1947, and their daughter, Joy Marie, was born there on November 30,
1951. The children were active in De Molay and Jobs' Daughters, respectively. Joy serving as Honored Queen of Bethel N o. 51 during her
father's term as Grand Master.
It was in 1946 that Gene received his first appointment to the faculty
of the U .C. School of Medicine, serving as an assistant, then as instructor, assistant clinical professor, associate clinical professor, and finally
as Clinical Professor, with additional responsibility as Chief of the Ear,
Nose and Throat Service of the San Francisco General Hospital. He has
served his profession with distinction, receiving honors from numerous
honor societies in his fleld, and served on the Board of D irectors of the
Sa.n Francisco Medical Society and as a delegate to the California Medical Association.
He is the author of numerous articles in his medical specialty and is
the inventor of an instrument for examination of the larynx.
Dr. Hopp has served his community in many capacities, such as member of the Board of Directors of Goodwill Industries, Chairman of the
Educatlon section of the Commonwealth Club and as Quarterly Chair ...
man of that Club, chalrman of the Professional D ivision of the United
Crusade, and as bead of his neighborhood improvement association. In
1964 he received the Honor Certifkate Award of the Freedom Foundation at Valley Forge in recognition of a Memorial Day address delivered
in San Francisco.
ill

His Masonic service has been equally notable. He was raised in
Lebanon Lodge No. 495 on July 19, 1947, serving as its Master in 1956.
He was Master of Northern California Research Lodge in 1959. He affiliated with King Solomon's Lodge No. 260 and is a Past Master of the
consolidated King Solomon's Seaport Lodge No. 260.
He has been active in both Scottish Rite and York Rite. He received
the honorary Knight Commander of the Court of Honor of the Scottish
Rite in 1963 and Knight Templar Cross of Honor in 1968. He was High
Priest of California Chapter No. 5, R.A.M . and later president of the
Keystone York Rite Association. He is a member of California Commandery No. I. K.T., a member of the Order of the Red Cross of Constantine, St. Francis Conclave, and of Islam Temple, A.A.0. N.M.S. He
is the author of many Masonic papers, such as the pamphlet of Grand
Lodge on "The Laying of Cornerstone s," and the publication of the
Masonic Service Association, "Let Freedom Ring." As a speaker on
different Masonic subjects he has always been much in demand.
Gene served the Grand Lodge for many years, as Chairman of the
Board of Library Commissioners, Chairman of the Masonic Education
Committee, member of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes,
and in 1963 served as Grand Orator. He was elected Junior Grand Warden in 1965. Senior Grand Warden in 1966 and Grand Master on October 13, 1967. At the 1968 Conference of Grand Masters of North America, at Washington , D. C., he delivered the key-note address, and his
"Man and Masonry" has been widely reprinted and acclaimed.
During his year as Grand Master, he challenged Master Masons in
California and Hawaii to rededicate themselves to the fundamental principles of Freemasonr y. His conduct as a man and a Mason has exemplified his own dedication, just as his labors in Freemasonr y have manifested his deep and abiding love for our great Fraternity.

I told all my jokes last night. I want to get down to serious busines s.
know your underta kings here are of the utmost seriousn ess.
I've been thinking about texts from the Scriptu res which would be
appropr iate for this occasio n, and I'd like to use two. First, these word,~
of Jesus: "Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
And then by way of contras t to that remark, this question raised by
Pilate as he wrung his hands in indecisi on and despair and cried out
.
' 'What is truth?"
As a nation I think we display very often a certain ineptne ss, even
a kind of pervers ity, in our quest of truth-o ur desire to see things as
they really are. to assess things, to evaluate . We hear the phrase. ''Tell
it like it is," and we are anxious indeed to see it as it is, and then to be
able to "tell it like it is."
I have two purpose s this mornin g-one, to attempt in my way to
outline the dimensi ons of some of the major problem s which face our
genera tion-an d secondl y, to take a brief look into the future at some
of the problem s which are moving , even now, to the center stage of
man's concern .
There are. of course. the continu ing massive problem s of war.
racism, poverty , etc. We can't cover all these or even attempt to, but
we can list certain of the issues which are going to be close to us as
Masons , and as citizens , and as particip ants and believer s in our various
religiou s persuas ions.
I'd like to call attentio n to the curious disparit y pointed out by my
distingu ished predece ssor in this office last year-th e way that we
refuse to see it like it is in relation to our nationa l wealth. I'm sure that
everyon e here could make a pretty good guess about our gross nationa
l
produc t-our income. All of us could make mention of the standar d of
living that we enjoy- how many radios, TV's, miles of telephon e wires.
and miles of roads. We could describe the charitie s and welfare activities of the governm ent. We know that we are a rich country .
How many of us know. as we attempt to see it as it is, that we spend
nearly three times as much on cosmeti cs as we spend on churche s and
all other charitab le organiz ations combin ed-and that the nationa
l
gamblin g bill, which is $33 billion, is approxi niately equal to the total
bill for educatio n in this country for one year, kinderg arten through
college. I'm not here to knock gamblin g as such-th at's a separat
e
kettle of fish. But it is interest ing that we should have this kind of
similari ty of figure- $33 billion for one thing-$ 33 billion for another
.
We have the unsolve d ethical problem of the use of wealth in connection with war. Here again, I'm not on the podium to attack the governmen t's point of view on war-I' m as tom and as heartsic k as anyone
on this subject. But this feeling cannot serve to blind us to the financia
l
realities which are that in Caesar' s time it cost 75 cents to kill an enemy
soldier. By the time of the Napoleo nic Wars the figure had risen to

7

$3.000 per dead enemy soldier. In the Civil War it cost $5.000. Senator
H. T. Bone has estimate d that in World War I it was $21 ,000-W orld
War II. $50,00 0-and now it may be costing, we are told. as much as
half a million dollars for each dead soldier on the other side of the battle
line. At the same time it costs about $1.500 a year to provide a young
man with a good college educatio n. We could send a whole cou ntry to
college for four years-m an, woman, child-f or what it costs to engage
in war year by year.
The steward ship of wealth -I think Masons have a particul ar
obligati on to study these figures -to work upon them, to try to interpre
t
them.
My Senior Warden , who is a kind of Senior Deacon in our Church .
once told me, "Figure s don't lie, but liars figure." He said to me once,
"Remem ber, Max, that a man can drown while crossing a stream which
average s only two feet in depth. Also," he said. ''if one man can build
a house in I 2 days, I 2 men can build it in one day, 288 men can build
it in one hour, and 17,280 workers can finish the job in one minute."
While we admit that there is indeed the possibil ity for distortio n in
figures , there is also the very great possibility that the figures w hich
we're thinking about show in blunt, unargua ble terms some of the d isquieting realities which we would like to avoid facing. We w ould like to
avoid seeing things as they really are.
In our quest for truth-h ere again, as Masons and as citizens-we
need an accurat e and honest evaluati on of the attacks upon the major
instituti ons of our society. I think, for example , of the educatio nal institution we know as 'the Univers ity of Californ ia. I am sure everyon
e
here knows that Eldridg e Cleaver is speakin g there. I am sure th at
everyon e knows there was a fellow named Mario Savio a coup le of
years back who raised a little Cain over there. I wonder if all o f us
do know that there were 791 Peace Corps volunte ers from the University of Californ ia in one year-tw ice the number of any university or
college in the United States. I wonder if people know in general that
the Univers ity of Californ ia student body support s out of its own
student money and funds an orphana ge in coopera tion with a M a rine
unit in Danang in Viet Nam. I wonder if they can tell that there are
600 volunte ers doing all kinds of good work in law, teaching . etc., in
coopera tion with commun ity educato rs and teachers . We don't really
see it as it is when we look at the Univers ity of Californ ia. And granted
that press commun ications , etc .. are difficult, we have the obligation and
we have the tools of the trade-- in Mason ry-to take us beyond the
superficial, quick, light look at our instituti ons and try to figure out in
some depth what is going on.
What's going on? It is indeed difficult to say, but one thing is
change. Change we've always had. I'm carryin g in my notes a little
saying that was carved by a slave on a stone 300 years before the

8

GRAND LODGE Of' CAUE'ORNIA

Christian era. He said: "Children do not obey their parents." W ell .
you can find echoes of this kind of remark all down through the centuries to this present generation , and in finding them often one might
be led to think that in spite of everythin g we will somehow get along.
just as we always have. Not so. There is a new kind of geometric progression in idea change which mass communic ation has made possible.
We know, also, that the population moves at a rate that frightens us.
We know that there is great change involved in the economics of th is,
but we don' t know exactly what to make of it. As Masons, as citizens,
we are called to think more than s uperficia lly about these very great
issues of the time.
There is in this present world a backlash against individual is m.
E veryone who knows the history of this country knows the importanc e
of our philosoph y of individual ism and the contributi on that we as a
nation have made to the world. But people are saying more and more
that our institution s, whether they be political. religious or education al
institution s, must be so ordered as to plainly show that they are living
by the principles upon which they c.re believed to be founded a nd said
to be founded. The cager and even sometimes reckless manner in which
hypocrisy is challenge d in our schools. churches and governme ntal
agencies will serve, I hope, to sharpen the public conscience and make
us unwilling to compromi se our shared ideals. It's not enough to say
that we have ideals . We must put them into action, put wheels on them .
or they are simply dusty ideas which have no relevance.
And it is not proper for Masons to think that they are exempt from
the corrosive processes of change. Across the street is Grace Cathedral ,
and if you've rea d the history o f thnt place lately you know that there
may be some cracks beginning to appear in the concrete. There is a
shaking and a trembling and, as we consider Masonic ethics-th ose
which are particular ly concerned in the arts of Masonry -we know
that there are things in our own house that need to be rethought in
ethical terms. which need to be reestablish ed, retested- good things
can always stand exam ination. \Ve want to think about those things
in these days.
There is a new th ing on the ethical scene. which is to move away
from stress on ideals and use what is called situation ethics. This is a
technical term, but if the words "situation ethics" mean nothing to you,
I'd suggest that if it doesn 't mean somethin g to you before long you
may be out of the ball game. It's an important term necessary to understanding what's going on today.
And there is a significant change taking place as we go from spasmodic, voluntary gifts of charity in our society to support of agencies
which deal with these needs on the basis of justice.
There is an Old Testamen t ring about this modern cry. Ancient
Hebrew laws knew nothing of charity in the present secular definition.

and this is true of Judaism today. Grain was left in the fields, th ings
were shared. debts were forgiven- because it was the right thing to do.
The r ight to a free life. the r ight to employme nt, etc.-thes e are very,
very old ideas which are being dusted off by certain of the wild-eyed
youngsters and are now placed before us as a form of challenge.
The idea of charity as something optional on the part of a do~gooder
is not to be confused with the New Testamen t or ancient Hebrew concept of love. The familiar quotation, "Faith, hope and charity-th ese
three," should be accurately and honestly rendered: "Faith, hope and
love-t hes e three. And the greatest of these is love." Christian people.
among others. I'm glad to say, are trying to recover pristine attitudes as
they seek decent hea lth and housing, etc .. fo r all of our citizenry. The
fact that there are some very strong leftist groups may tempt us to turn
away from these considerat ions and these endeavors . but that would be
contrary to the vows that we have made to ourselves a nd to our God as
Mason5.
To our list of changes could be added such items as the rad ical
changes in theology. the new permissive ness. the new conscienti ous
objector, the stretching of doctrinal boundarie s and attitudes, the demand for freedom from ecclesiasti cal control. change in worship services. hippie love-ins- a ll within the vision of a thoroughl y secular
world. No one knows why so many and so great changes should be
jam-packe d into one generation . Only one th ing can be said for sure:
It is what's happening .

9

A study of the complex and only partly answered mora l questions
of today does not tend to make one feel that he is ready. com e w hat may,
for the questions of tomorrow, and rd like to think about some of them
very briefly. The questions are already here. They appear in every
endea vor, in every area of human life: medicine, spnce travel. education, family life. Again , in the manner of one scanning the horizon. let's
look quickly at some of these problems.
Consider the problems soon to be faced in human procreatio n. Testtube babies now live as long as two months. Does the scientist, knowing
that the embryo will certainly die, commit a kind of murder when he
starts a human life by fertilizing an egg in a test tube with a male sperm?
Or, is there a basic difference between the embryo nnd the more mature
foetus? Does a child become a human being at the moment of conception, at the time of the quickenin g of the foetus. or is this status ac hieved
at birth? If it happens at birth. when is the exact moment?
What about the wife whose husband is sterile? Artificial insemination is now a fairly common process- the egg produced by the wife is
fertilized by a sperm obtained through an anonymous male donor who
is "compatib le: · This procedure is under the direction of a qualified
physician. Now. is this adultery? An Archbisho p of England once said

10

PROCEEDINGS OP THB

it was. Should the husband in such a case feel that he is the father of
the child? Or, to look at it another way, must a couple have all of the
capacity for parenthood before they can experience some of the joy?
What is the Masonic definition which would apply here? Masonry is
an ethical society, among other things. We need to turn our thoughts
in these directions- to begin to answer questions which are coming
faster than we realize.
In the National Lutheran Magazine there is a report of the possibility of using chromosomes in any human cell as the basis of procreation. What. they ask, would this do to marital union? Who would
rule on genetic loans? What about the rights of individuals who desire
such procedures? Who would have the right to initiate chromosome
conception? Would this be more desirable, socially, than normal birth?
After a visi t to the marital counselor would the couple anticipating marriage go on to the genetic counselor? Is this a kind of a part of the
dream of the Nazis of the super-race? What is the role of the Church
here? What is the role of the State? What do Masons think? What
will Masons think? Unless they are thinking ahead, they won't think
anything.
Many of the not-yet-critical moral questions seem to be taken from
the pages of some outlandish science-fiction novel. Sooner than we
think, we shall have to face ethical problems involved in recent scientific
advances.
It will be possible, for example. for men's minds to be altered by
such things as chemical injections which will actually transmit knowledge-memory molecule transplants. Drug treatments will vastly accelerate the learning process. University of California at Los Angeles
scientists Ba bich. Jacobson and Bubash claim they have transferred
knowledge: from hamsters to rats by the injection of a certain acid,
RNA. from the brain of one animal to another. In a similar experiment
at U .C. scientists tell of transferring a "memory molecule: " from one
flatworm to another, so that the second animal knew what the first had
formerly known. A pharmaceutical manufacturer has developed a
compound that enables rats to learn five times faster, and the Food and
Drug Administration will soon have to decide whether to allow the use
of the compound in human beings.
And the day may not be far away when thousands of our citizens
wear "happy buttons," electrodes placed in the brain which can produce
a profound and instant effect on behavior. A man in a flt of rage could
press the button and receive: an electrical charge in a certain section of
his brain, and be immediately at peace with himself and the whole world.
And this is not out of science fiction-it's been done already. The
electrodes could be installed complete with batteries under the scalp and
they could be operated by remote control.

The possibilities of mind control have been increased with the discovery that certain types of mental illness can be brought on by the use
of drugs. A pound of LSD in the water reservoir of a small town could
keep the community disoriented for weeks. In a similar vein, scientists
claim that biological agents capable of destroying man's will to resist
are only 25 years away. Well, are we going to have such things as
electronic catechism, sleep learning? Who will push the buttons?
There is the question of contamination of space. One British scientist
has said, "What right do we have to take measles virus to the moon?"
And this coming at a time when Schirra is floating around above us
with a very bad head cold.
The knottiest problems will not come from the medical laboratories.
however. It is expected that push-button factories and farms of the
future will some day do away with the practical need to work, at least
work in the sense that we know it. "The superior man of the future,"
says one writer, "will be the person who can cope with a world without
work .• .. He will prize his ability to relax, to contemplate:, to attend to
the world around him, to create, to fashion, to be aware of his inner
feelings."
This kind of future may look rosy to some people. but what about
the man who likes to work? Is there substance in the biblical injunctions
which give religious meaning to work? Is the pleasure of work to be
~llowed only to a few? If this generation finally succeeds in getting
)Obs for everyone, and we're doing our best to achieve it, will the next
generation succeed in abolishing jobs for everyone? We have to think
about it.
•
The problems of our world are so weighty, so complex, that most
of us fall into a mood of despair and futility as we attempt to face them
and understand them. Most of us want to feel that our individual efforts
do count for something, yet we are in continual need of reassurance.
I have a brief word of reassurance from the pen of James A. Francis.
who sums up the story of one solitary life:
" Here is a young man who was born in an obscure village, the child
of a peasant woman. He grew up in another village. He worked in a
carpenter shop until he was 30. and then for three years he was an
itinerant preacher. He never wrote a book. He never held an office.
He never owned a home. He never had a family. He never went to
college. He never put his foot inside a big city. He never traveled 200
miles from the place where he was born. He never did one of the things
that usually accompany greatness. He had no credentials but himself.
"While he was still a young man, the tide of public opinion turned
against him. His friends ran away. He was turned over to his enemies.
He went through the mockery of a trial. He was nailed to a cross between two thieves. While he was dying. his executioners gambled for

the only piece of property he had on this earth, and that was his co~t.
When he was dead. he was laid in a borrowed grave through the pity
of a friend.
" Nineteen wide centuries have come and gone, and today he is the
central figure of the human race and a leader of the column of progress.
"I am far within the mark when I say that all the armies that ever
marched, and all the navies that were ever built, and all the parliaments
that ever sat. and all the kings that ever reigned, put together, have not
affected the life of man upon this earth as has that One single, Solitary
Life."
A poet puts it this way:
"You say the little efforts that I make
Will do no good;
They never will prevail
To tip the hovering scale
Where justice hangs in balance.
I don't think
I ever thought they would.
But I am prejudiced beyond debate
In favor of my right to choose which side
Shall feel the stubborn ounces of my weight."
As Masons. we do indeed have ounces. As a group we have pounds.
Let us in the challenging days ahead use this weight for the glory and
for the purposes o f God . Amen.

l nvocation- Necrology
Once again we are assembled to pay tribute to the memory of those
Brethren who have departed from our midst during the past year. While
we pay tribute to their memory. let us not do so in sadness but rather
in gratitude for the privilege that was ours to walk with them and to
witness the good deeds that they have wrought upon the trestleboard
of life. As Masons, we believe in God, and we have the certain assurance that they are now safe in our Father's house. Let us remember the
words of comfort by the Master to his disciples as they gathered around
him and the shadow of the cross was closing in, "Let not you r hearts be
troubled: Ye believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house
a re ma ny mansions: If it were not so. I would have told you. And if I go
and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you unto
myself. that where I am may ye be also."
Since the last convocation 438 Past Masters and Wardens of our
Grand Lodge have passed to their eternal reward. Time will not permit
the recounting of the many virtues and services to the craft of more than
a few. The death toll was heaviest in Chico Lodge No. 111 and Vermont

Duke Paoa K ahanamoku. Death came swiftly on January 23 of this
year to a most remarkable man and brother, Duke Paoa Kahana moku. a
member of Hawaiian Lodge No. 21. A gentle. kindly man of simple dignity, an honored public figure, and a beloved personal friend to the thousands of people who were privileged to know him . Of pure Polynesian
ancestry he was born in the old Arlington Hotel. now the location of
The Bank of Hawaii, at the corner of Bishop and King Streets in downtown Honolulu. This simple child of the sea was destined to become the
friend of kings and commoners alike, the world over. He was born in
troubled times, August 24, 1890. during the reign of Kin q Ka l<J kaua .
las t of the Hawaiian kings. followed by his sister, Queen Liliuokalani ,
the last royal ruler of the Hawaiian kingdom. He was but 4 years old
when the short lived Republic of Hawaii was set up, and on July 7th.
1898, automatical ly became an American citizen when the American
flag was raised over the islands. unknown to most of the world. little
specks in the broad Pacific. In 1911, this hitherto unknown beach boy
electrified the entire athletic world when in an AA U swimming meet,
held in Honolulu , he broke the long standing 100 yard world sprint
record by an astonishing 4-3/ 5 seconds. All eyes were foc used on
Hawaii and the old days were over. During his lifetime H awaii was to
emerge from a slttpy Polynesian kingdom to the great commonwea lth
that we know today.
He became its unofficial am bassador as he toured the world setting
new records and w inning countless friends wherever he traveled. First
1912 and the Stockholm Olympiad, new world records ; more gold medals; then home to a hero's welcome. His modest demeanor and athletic
prowess had won the hearts of people the world over. This hitherto almost unknown land and its people overnight became of interest to the
whole world. Hawaii could ask no more of him. The years rolled by. the
1920 Antwerp Olympiad. Paris in 1924, Los Angeles in 1932. the only
man. save one. to ever qualify for such a number. Only World War.
1916. robbed him of a fifth Olympiad. June 1925 brought tragedy and the
supreme effort of his remarkable career. Duke was camping on the
beach at Corona Del Mar. 50 miles south of Los Angeles, with a party
of friends, when the yacht Thelma capsized in a heavy surf. With the
first sign of trouble, the Duke and his surfboard were on their way. He
made three trips through the rag ing surf. Seventeen lives were lost that
day and 12 persons rescued. D uke saved eight. The territory of Hawaii
struck a gold medal in his honor. The papers acclaimed his performance
as the most superhuman rescue act and the finest display of surfboard

riding ever seen in this world. The years rolled on. more fame, heartaches. ill health. Sheriff of Honolulu for 25 years and in the final years,
its official greeter. The sands were running out, yet honor upon honor
were heaped on him. When people saw or heard his name they thought
of Hawaii. He was truly the D uke of Hawaii, the land he loved so well.
that he wanted the whole world to share it with him. Governor John A .
Burns, at Duke's dea th, among other remarks said-"More than any
other man in our modem history, Duke embodied all that is fine and
ennobling in our Hawaiian culture. He reflected great credit and honor
to our Polynesian people. His humility and the dignity which characterized his life shall remain an inspiration for all our citizens. We shall
miss D uke as we miss few others whose friendship we were privileged
to enjoy."
Our brother was singularly attuned to the tenets of Freemasonry,
and his character and life, epitomized the pure principles of our order.
Raised in Hawaiian Lodge No. 21 on October 30, 1946, he immediately
embraced Masonry with the same zest and zeal that characterized his
every endeavor. He continued his Masonic career in the Scottish Rite
Bodies of Honolulu, where he received the rank and decoration of Knight
Commander of the Court of H onor. serving as Master of Kadosh in
1957. He also became a member of the Royal Arch, Royal & Select
Masters, Knights Templar and Aloha Temple of the Shrinl", where he
was most active in raising funds for the Hospital for Crippled Children.
His funeral was attended by thousands of every creed and from
every walk of life. At the conclusion of the Cathedral Services, the
funeral procession with his ashes moved to the Royal Hawaiian as the
flags of the Commonwealth stood at half mast. in honor of her most
famous son. On the beach, the urn containing his ashes was placed on a
surfboard atop his own red and white outrigger canoe, with his Masonic
apron and two white carnation leis. As thousands of tourists and friends
thronged the beach and every point o f vantage, Worshipful Master
Howard Wong performed the Masonic Rites, followed by the simple
beach boy service. As the funeral party embarked, black clouds formed
over D iamond Head. His widow, Nadine, sitting with his urn resting
in her lap, the procession moved out beyond the reef where the Revenue
Cutter Corwin waited. Her entire crew at attention, the final words of
commitment were spoken as his widow tenderly put the urn over the side
of the canoe and thousands of flower petals were scattered on the water.
To quote from Mark Anthony's funeral oration, in Shakespeare's Julius
Caesar, "His life was so gentle, and the elements so mixed in him that
nature might stand up and say to all the world. 'This was a man'."

Brother Stephen Edward Skidmore was born in Downey, Californ ia ,
on August 4th, 1881. and passed to his eternal rest on November 4th,
1967. He was raised in Azusa Lodge No. 305 on March 17, 1914. serving as its Master in 1911. He served the Grand Lodge as Grand Chaplain in 1946 and thereafter as Inspector of District No. 608 from 1947
to 1961. He was Master of Upland Lodge No. 419 in 1924, and at the
time of his death was a plural member of Lexington Lodge No. 104 in
El Monte. H is fraternal activities included Azusa Chapter of the Royal
Arch, Jasmine Chapter of the Eastern Star and Pasadena Consistory of
the Scottish Rite.
Brother Ralph Benton Saffle was a native of Alma. Kansas, where
he was born July 9th, 1907. He served his country in the U .S. Navy
during W orld W ar II. Settling in Long Beach, he became active in veteran affairs, serving as Commander of Veterans of Foreign Wars, Golden State Post. He was raised in Service Lodge No. 594 in 1919 and
served as its Master in 1965 . He was a member of the Grand Lodge
Constitution Observance Committee in 1967 and died on January 7th
of this year. He is .survived by his wife Rita.

John Virgil Bacigalupi. In the passing of Brother John Virgil Bacigalupi, the Grand Lodge of California has lost one of its most stalwart
members. He was born in San Francisco on December 1, 1895. A banker
by profession, in which he served the Bank of America at San Rafael
as a vice president and manager for 43 years until his retirement in 1961.
He passed away March 29th in Catania, Italy, where he was vacationing.

William E. Bouton. Death, as it must to all men, came to Brother
William E. Bouton at the age of 92 on Friday night, June 21st. 1968,
at St. Francis Hospital in San Francisco following a lingering illness.
A native son born in Oakland in 1876, his entire life was spent in
and around San Francisco, where on January 6th, 1900, he was united
in marriage with his wife, Minnie, who survives him; also 3 daughters,
5 grandchildren and 5 great-grandchildren. He was for many years
engaged in the building and loan business in San Francisco and later on
established his own insurance business.
He was made a member of Occidental Lodge No. 22 of San Francisco September 30th, 1907, serving as its Master in 1942. He also
served his Lodge as Secretary from 1944 through 1965. He was a member of the Royal Arch and the California Bodies of the Scottish Rite,
which he joined in 1914, and received the honor and decoration of Knight
Commander of the Court of Honor in 1954. He served as Wise Master
of the Chapter Rose Croix in 1933 and Master of Kadosh of the Consistory in 1943.
Brother Hillard Merton Reeves, a member of McKinley Lodge No.
437 of Richmond, was born in the year 1917 in Buhl. Idaho. Graduating
from the University of California at Berkeley, he was appointed Criminologist for the City of Richmond Police Department in 1949. He was
a founder and first president of the California Order of Patrolmen. He
was also a member of California Association of Criminalists, Contra
Costa County Peace Officers Association, and the East Bay Municipal
Employees Union.
He was made a Master Mason in McKinley Lodge No. 347 November 8th, 1956, and served as its Master in 1964. He was appointed Inspector of the I 20th Masonic District in 1966, in which capacity he was
serving with distinction at the time of his death. He is survived by his
wife, Elizabeth, and daughter, Susan.
A man highly esteemed by all who knew him and in the words of
his friend and Secretary of McKinley Lodge, Brother Peter Slavazza,
"He was a man to ride the river with."

He was made a Master Mason in Marin Lodge No. 191, on March
3rd, 1938, serving as its Master in 1947. Subsequently. on many of its
committees, he was a member of the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance, 1947-48, and subsequently, for approximately 18 years, on the
"Pay of Members" Committee.
He was a member of many Masonic affiliated bodies: Marin Chapter
No. 10, R.A.M.; Redwood Empire Council No. 46, Royal & Select
Masters; Marin Commandery No. 73, Knights Templar; Islam Temple
of the Shrine; Pyramid Temple No. 31 of the Sciots, etc.
He is survived by his wife, Ruby, three sisters and a brother.
He was a true and faithful Brother, a great Mason, a fine citizen and
a devoted husband and father. We leave him in the hands of our Supreme Grand Master, thankful for the years which were given to him
to serve with us in the furtherance of Masonry.

Brother Horace Scott Seaton, a member of Charter Rock Lodge No.
410 of Berkeley, now consolidated with Berkeley Lodge No. 363, passed
to his well earned rest on June 3rd, 1968 and was a member of the Graft
for 76 years. A reception was given in his honor in 1967, at which time
he was presented with his 75 year pin by Grand Master Laurence E.
Dayton. There is only one other living 75 year member of the Grand
Lodge of California.
Brother Gladney Lee Hamilton served the Grand Lodge as Grand
Bible Bearer in 1957. A native of Texas he came to California as a young
man, settling in Delano, where for over twenty years he was office manager for the 5,000 acre Sierra Farms. Active in community life, he embraced Masonry in 1946 and was made a Master Mason in Delano
Lodge No. 309 in that year. He served as its Master in 1953. He is
survived by his wife, Berniece, and daughters, Judy and Jana.
Brother George Rhine Meyering was a member of Las Palmas
Lodge No. 366 of Fresno, where he was raised April 21, 1921, serving
as its Master in 1928. He was born in Muskegon, Michigan, January 17,
1886. He served Grand Lodge as Senior Grand Steward in 194 7-48 and
on the Masonic Homes Endowment Board in 1950-52. His fraternal
activities included the Scottish Rite, Royal Arch. Knights Templar and
the Shrine. He is survived by his wife, Mattie, and one son.

Brother Walter Frederick Flierl was a member of Eucalyptus Lodge
No. 243 of Hayward, where he passed away January 30th of this year,
A native son, our Brother was born in Oakland December 16, 1891, and
lived all his life in Alameda County. He was raised in Acorn Lodge No.
494, May 27th, 1922, and served as its Master in 1937. He served the
Grand Lodge on the DeMolay Committee for four years. Past President
of the Alameda County Historical Society and active member of the
First Presbyterian Church, he had many interests in civic affairs. Fraternally he was a member of the Oakland Scottish Rite Bodies and
Aahmes Temple of the Shrine.

Brother Charles Elias Sones. To have known him was truly a gift of
God, a gift which would enrich the life of anyone.
Charles Elias Sones was born near Lacona, Iowa, on December 8.
1888. Moving to the Imperial Valley as a young man. he became active
in the lumber business.
He was made a Master Mason of El Centro Lodge No. 384 on June
22. 1914, and served as its Worshipful Master in 1925. He was actiYe
in the First Methodist Church of El Centro, served as that city's mayor
and for nineteen vears served on the school board of the El Centro
School District and was a Past President of the El Centro Rotary Club.
He was honored by the Supreme Council, 33° of the Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. by being coronated a 33° of
the Scottish Rite. He was a member of the Red Cross of Constantine, a
Past Commander Knights Templar. a member of the Royal Arch. He
served on the Grand Lodge Credentials Committee 1934-38 and on the
By-Laws 1960-61. He was Senior Grand Steward of this Grand Lodge
1940-41. At the time of his passing on August 16, 1967, he had been a
Master Mason for fifty-three years. He is survived by his wife, Carrie,
together with a son and daughter. "The Lord has given and the Lord
has taken away-Blessed be the name of the Lord."
Brother Egbert Andrew Hc1dson was a Past Master of Paso Robles
Lodge No. 286. He passed away on December 27, 1967.
We honor his memory not as a Past Grand Officer but rather for
the many contributions which he made to our fraternity, perhaps the
most notable being the beautiful model of King Solomon's Temple
which he built and presented to this Grand Lodge and which may now
be seen in the lobby. He also presented an electric train set complete
with track. modeled mountains, communities. etc., to the Home at Union
City for our senior guests' enjoyment.
Such brethren as Egbert Hudson who have given sacrificially of
themselves will live in our memory long after their departure. in that
celestial lodge above where the Supreme Grand Master of the universe
forever presides.
Brother Thomas Francis Mason . A great man was lost to our fraternity in the passing of this Past Master of Wilmington Lodge No. 198,
who passed to his well earned reward on March I st of this year. Born
in Cheyenne, Wyoming, on March 7, 1882. he moved to Southern California at an early age and settled in Wilmington. where he became
active in many organizations, rising to the top office in most of them.
serving all with noted distinction.
He was a man of tremendous drive and superior mental ability. yet
modest in deportment. He was made a Master Mason in Wilmington
Lodge No. 198 in January of 1921. He passed his proficiency on March

8th and acted as Master. conferring all three degrees within four months
after his raising. He served Wilmington Lodge as its Master in 1925.
He was appointed Senior Grand Deason 1939-40. Subsequently he
served on the Credentials Committee 1950-65 and Pay of Members
Committee 1966.
A member of many affiliated Masonic Bodies including the Royal
Arch. Royal and Select Masters. Knights Templar, Al Malaikah Temple
of the Shrine and served the Job's Daughters and DeMolay for many
years in an advisory capacity. He is survived by his wife. Eva Gay. and
three sons.

Brother Patrick ]. Tliompsett. Master Mason. devoted husband.
loving father, how can mere words convey to those of us who loved him
our sense of loss in parting from this devoted Brother. Raised in South
Pasadena Lodge No. 367 on May 26th. 1936. he began a Masonic career
of service which never slackened for more than thirty yea.rs. He served

He is survived by his widow. Emily, daughters. Pat and Jackie, and
son Mike.

Brother]. Howard Edwards served as Senior Grand Deacon during
1949-50, the centennial year of our Grand Lodge. and established an
enviable record in that office. He participated not only in the annual
communications but in every special cummunication to lay a cornerstone.
dedicate a hall, or constitute a new lodge whether held in the southern
or northern parts of the state. His presence at every reception tendered
the Grand Master from Fresno to San Diego added to those occasions.
Brother Edwards was born in North Carolina and came to Los Angeles when he was twenty-two years of age. The year 1924 was a significant one in his life. for in addition to coming west he became a member
of the Los Angeles Police Department and was joined in marriage with
Evelyn Peterson. His affiliation with the Police Department was to be
for the next twenty- four years, his residence for forty years and the
marriage for life.
In 1937 he received our degrees in Progressive Lodge. Los Angeles.
and ten years later served as its Master; thereafter he served as officers'
coach for five years and on four of the lodge committees. He was elected

On Tuesday morning the Grand Master. pursuant to the stress in
recent years toward Masonic encouragement and interest in youth activities and particularly in keeping with his own feelings in this regard,
called down Grand Lodge and had escorted to the East the following
representatives of youth organizations who delivered the addresses
below:
Gayle Stiltner, Honored Queen, Grand Bethel of Job's Daughters" Who is a Job's Daughter? A Job's Daug her is a girl approaching
womanhood who has a Masonic heritage.
Girls are eligible for membership in Job's Daughters at the age of 12
and reach majority membership at age 20 or when married. Each girl
must have a relationship to a Master Mason in good standing or who
was in good standing at the time of his death.
At 12 years. girls are still developing character. A Job's Daughter

GRAND MASTER's GoLD BurroN-SPECIAL PRESENTATION

Inspector Robert W. Dunwoody of District No. 402, on behalf of
Summit Lodge No. 112, presented a new Grand Master's button to
Grand Master Hopp. In making the presentation he read the following
summary:
"Gold fever has struck the hearts of men for centuries and ages
long since past. Today gold mining is almost an extinct skill here in
America, but each year the brethren of Summit Lodge No. 112, F.&A.M.
are affiicted with this ancient and highly contagious disease as they
gather their picks, shovels, pans and sluices when they journey into the
still gold-rich hills of colorful Northern California.

In an area near the historic town of Knights Ferry, in the eastern
foothill country of Stanislaus County, they assemble to perform their
venerable rite. The call of "gold" still creates a surge of excitement in
the hearts of these men. Thus it was in the spring of 1968, when Grand
Master Eugene S. Hopp suggested that Summit Lodge mine the necessary gold and create from it a new Grand Master's lapel pin to be passed
from Grand Master to Grand Master. The response from the members of
the Lodge was one of affirmative enthusiastic unanimity.
Needless to say, it didn't take long for brethren to mine the required
amount of the precious metal to make the pin, because they have been
doing this sort of thing for many, many years. It has been a tradition
among the members to mine the gold for their Past Master's jewels for
presentation each year at the Installation of Officers Ceremony to their
outgoing Master.
It is with great honor and pride that the new Grand Master's pin,
made from pure California Mother Lode Gold. is presented to our Most
Worshipful Grand Master at the 1968 proceedings of the Grand Lodge
of California.
The pin itself was made by Summit Lodge Past Master William L.
Waggle. It was cast in sand from clay of the same variety found in the
clay grounds of Jordan. No modern tools were used and it was hand
carved. The raw nugget. representing the rough ashlar, was contributed
by the former Inspector of the 402nd Masonic District, Claiborn E.
Schonhoff. An alloy of gold and brass creates the yellow background.
The rose color is the result of the combining of copper, brass and gold. A
combination of gold and silver provides the mountings for the three
diamonds. A close examination of the pin will disclose a number of
Masonic symbols. The crack near the letter "C" is emblematic of the
destruction of King Solomon's Temple."
The Grand Master expressed the appreciation of the Grand Lodge
of California and expressed the assurance that future Grand Masters
would wear the pin with pride and satisfaction.

Grand M aster's Gold Button
Presented by Summit Lodge No. 112
Monday, October 1-t, 1968

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
On October 13, I 967 you, my Brethren, placed in my hands the great
responsibility of carrying out the tremendous duties and obligations of
this Grand Lodge and also charged me with observing your will in
accordance with the actions taken during the 1967 Communication .
Today, I am to render an account of that stewardship.
The task presented in I 967 seemed almost insurmountable for this
office had just been vacated by a dedicated, conscientious , able and
hard-working Grand Master and it was obvious that it would be virtually impossible to equal his footsteps, let alone follow them.
As I looked about the Temple on that Friday afternoon and saw,
at least in my mind's eye, all those distinguished Past Grand Masters
who had served this Grand Lodge so well and who had contributed so
much of themselves toward making this Grand Lodge one of the most
respected and admired in the world, I suddenly felt most humble and I
silently prayed for divine guidance and assistance.
How well I have completed my labors is for you, my Brethren, and
time to judge. I can but acknowledge the invaluable assista nce of our
Past Grand Masters throughout the year, and the warmth of your
Brotherhood and fraternal assistance whenever and wherever you were
requested to participate in the task before us. For the pleasure and honor
of these experiences I shall be eternally grateful.

Within a week after the commencement of this Masonic year, I
caused to be circulated to all the Lodges a message calculated to clarify
the action of Grand Lodge at its 1967 communication with regard to
the liquor question. The message pointed out that since all proposed
legislation had been rejected, there was no change in the law and the
directive of Grand Master Dayton of October 26, 1966 was still in force.
Despite the widest possible dissemination of this information, it has been
necessary to order a strict observance of our law in several instances
among prerequisite organizations.
MASONIC HOMES

This year your support for our Masonic Homes has surpassed that
of the previous year by more than $8,000.00 and for that I know I
express the thanks of your less fortunate Brethren and their families who
are the beneficiaries of your contributions. The complete report of the
devoted activities of the Trustees of our Homes will be presented by the
President of the Board, Past Grand Master Alfred Breslauer. You
should be advised, however, of the momentous decisions made by the
Board in recent years which have finally resulted in their becoming able
to broaden the admission requirements and to accept guests for the
Homes they could not previously accept because of State law. The
Board has long felt that some means should be found to admit to the
~omes those who required the environment which these residences pro,
v1ded so well. In the past, the State Department of Social Wel£are
permitted only ambulatory residents at the Home at Decoto. After thor,
oughly reviewing the situation with representatives of the State Welfare
Department and the State Fire Marshal. the Board received permission
to admit non,ambulatory residents to the third and fourth floors of
Adams Hall. The Board is to be congratulated on this expansion of
needed service to the Craft.
In April, I was asked whether or not a Lodge could contribute to
the Masonic Homes Christmas Fund. It was contended that since the
Code did not prohibit the donation, it was not illegal and that since
Homes Superintendents had accepted such donations in the past, Lodge
action had thus been approved. I had to express my opinion that neither
of these contentions could be supported. Section 409 of the California
Masonic Code provides that a Lodge shall not use or permit use of its
funds "for any other thing whatsoever except, in its discretion, it may
make expenditures hereinafter permitted."
Since further, it had been held that Lodge funds may not be contributed to many worthy causes (Sections 409 m, 410 a, 412 1, 409 n)
and since in prior years Grand Lodge resolution was required to
authorize such things as contributions from the refreshment fund to
the Memorial Temple (Section 412 t) or to the Endowment Fund in

38

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

place of floral pieces for deceased persons (Section 411) I had to render
the opinion that the contribution could not be made. I pointed out clearly
that funds can be used for presents or clothing for Lodge dependents in
the Home (Section 409 aa and Section 409 ac) although they could not
be used to pay an item such as the insurance premium on the life of a
boy in the home (Section 409 h). I also pointed out that there was
nothing to prevent individual contributions by members of the Lodge.
Feeling, however, very keenly that the idea of the contribution by a
Lodge to the Masonic Homes Christmas Fund was an excellent one, I
communicated my opinion in the matter to the Homes Board of Trustees
and in response to my request they have introduced Resolution No. 10
which provides that contributions to the Masonic Homes Christmas
Fund by any Lodge from moneys in its refreshment fund shall be deemed
to be for the promotion of fraternal intercourse within the meaning of
Section 412 of the California Masonic Code. This resolution will be
before you for consideration at this session. I cannot urge strongly
enough that you approve this resolution which will provide for the practice of remembering our guests at the Homes during the holiday season.
This practice, in my opinion, is one that should be augmented and not
discontinued.
Because of the great program of the Investment Committee of
Grand Lodge under the very able and dedicated direction of our Grand
Treasurer. Paul A. Pflueger, the Homes Trustees were able this year
to recommend a reduction of 35¢ in the per capita for the Homes. The
Trustees are to be congratulated and if each Lodge redoubles its effort
on behalf of the Homes Endowment Fund the per capita could undoubtedly be reduced even further.
ELIGIBILITY OF APPLICANTS

Under the question of the eligibility of applicants, Grand Master
Laurence E. Dayton at the 1967 Communication discussed the question
of the effect of a previous conviction of crime on the eligibility of a man
to apply for the Degrees of Masonry. His Recommendation No. 5
adopted by Grand Lodge reads as follows: ''That the Committees on
Polioy and General Purposes and on Jurisprudence be requested jointly
to restudy this entire subject and to propose legislation for consideration
at the 1968 Annual Communication which (a) more clearly defines
policy, and ( b) establishes adequate guidelines for implementing the
same."
The two committees designated have studied the problem and they
have recommended as a matter of policy that no person who has pleaded
guilty or nolo contendere to or been convicted of a felony or a misdemeanor which is morally wrong s hall be eligible for the Degrees of
Masonry unless such conviction shall have been vacated or set aside

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

39

or unless the applicant shall have been pardoned for the reason that he
did not commit the crime.
The two committees noted that with the exception of the provision
relating to the vacation of a judgment of conviction and the matter of
pardon, this general polic·y determination was enacted into Masonic law
by a 5/ 6 vote of Grand Lodge in 1957 and is now contained in Section
511-o of the California Masonic Code.
Appropriate legislation to be proposed by the Committee on Jurisprudence will carry out the effects of these reco mmendations. I urge its
adoption. I firmly believe that the test of morality in a crime is a most
proper one for determination of an applicant's eligibility.
BOA RDS OF RELIEF

In Recommendation No. 4 Grand Master Dayton recommended "an
exhaustive study of sojourner relief and the Board of Relief System."
This was adopted by Grand Lodge with the change that a special committee be appointed to formu late recommendations and present their
findings for consideration this year. A very able committee has devo ted a
year of study to the problem and has uncovered many and va rying problems a nd multiple ramifications associated with this study. The Committee in its report to me pointed out that providing relief for sojourning
Masons, their widows and orphans, was a most proper func tion of the
Boards of Relief but that over the years, additional functions have been
assumed partly, undoubtedly, because they were vital func tions which
needed to be performed but which were not indeed wi thin the true
province of the Board of Relief. These functions included the opera tion
of a blood bank, the making of sick calls, the granting of awards and
the conducting of funerals which is certainly more properly the fu nction
of a Lodge.
P ractices throughout our Grand Jurisdiction with regard relief var y
considerably. Some Boards have solicited bequests and have received
very large sums of money; one recent bequest being in the amount of
$50,000.00.
In addition to the foregoing problems which will require resolution,
the questions asked by Grand Master Dayton in his message on this
subject of sojourner relief will, of course, require more detailed study
and specific a nswers. The questions ra ised include the present nature and
extent of the relief needs of so journers ; the distribution of the problem
geographically; the effect or the possible effect of such programs as
Social Security. Disability and Unemploy ment Insurance nnd other Federa l programs and StLtte programs up on the problems. This committee
must ~ome to gr ips with the answer to the question, "What is the proper
funct10n of a Board of Relief?" S ho11ld this be a program of Grand
Lodge and how should the finn ncial hmden he distributed ;;irnong th('
Lodges?

conceiva bly could be involved. I asked our Junior Grand Warden , Herbert A. Huebner , a noted patent attorney, to serve as Chairma n. The
Committ ee itself was compose d of the Grand Treasure r; the Chairma n
of the Finance Committ ee, another Past Grand Master; and an Assistant Grand Lecturer, a member of the Ritual Committ ee. The committee
very carefully reviewed the detailed studies made by the Finance Committee. It consulte d with and met with Grand Lodge officers, Inspecto rs,
Committ ee Chairme n, Board Chairme n, and circulari zed by question naire, Inspecto rs and Committ ee and Board Chairme n, to endeavo r to
determin e and clarify current practices with the purpose of determin ing
those practices which" were in the best interests of Freemas onry. This
committe e has prepared for your consider ation a very fine and comprehensive report which was mailed to all the Lodges in August so that
there might be adequate review and discussio n of the recomme ndations .

I have also examine d the operation of our Board of Relief system in
connecti on with the blood bank service and learned that practices in
blood banking vary consider ably.
I received a letter from a Master of a Lodge regardin g one Masonic
blood bank of a Board of Relief in which I was advised that funds col~
lected for the blood bank were being diverted to the operation of the
Board of Relief or that the income from funds provided for a blood bank
were being so used. I promptly replied that in my opinion, neither funds
nor the interest on funds donated by members of Lodges through such
Lodges to the blood bank reserve account to cover the cost of purchasi ng
blood or for promotio n could be put in the general fund for operatio n of
a Board of Relief. I pointed out that these were trust funds donated for
a specific purpose and could not be diverted to the general funds of the
Board of Relief for its operation .
I have also discusse d the matter of blood banks with the Executiv e
Secretar y of our San Francisc o Medical Societi)' Blood Bank and I have
been advised that it would be possible to establish a blood bank for our
entire Grand Ju1'isdiction which would enable Master Masons and their
families to receive blood almost anywher e in the world, by means of a
phone call authoriza tion or letter to a central office perhaps in the Grand
Lodge.
RecoMME NDATION No. 2

I therefore recomme nd that a special committe e continue the study
of sojourne r relief and the entire Board of Relief system with a particular view to recomme nding to Grand Lodge at its next Annual Commun ication. the manner of organiza tion of relief; what areas shall be covered beyond those of sojourne r relief. if any; how these boards shall be
maintain ed financially and how blood banks shall be organize d.

RECOMM ENDATIO N No. 3
SPEOAL FI NANCE STUDY

At the I 966 Annual Commun ication of this Grand Lodge. the recommendatio n of then Grand Master Myron E. Smith was adopted that
"the Finance Committ ee of the Grand Lodge be requeste d to make a
compreh ensive study and review of the whole subject of expendit ures of
Lodge funds and Grand Lodge funds ... and to submit its findings and
recomme ndations at the next Annual Commun ication." Our Finance
Committ ee did indeed conduct a very compreh ensive and able study
which pointed out a number of areas in which the practices varied among
the constitue nt Lodges and in Grand Lodge with regard expendit ures.
In 1967, G rand l\faster Dayton pointed out that '"remedial measures
to achieve more equitable and consisten t practices at both levels are

I recomme nd that the report of the Special Finance Study Committ ee
be adopted in principle and that the Special Finance Study Committ ee
be requeste d to prepare the necessar y rules and regulatio ns to impleme nt
the recomme ndations of the report and that these shall be effective upon
approval by the Grand Master. Those recomme ndations of the Special
Finance Study Committ ee which require changes in our law shall have
these changes in the law prepared by the Committ ee with the assistanc e
of the Jurisprud ence Committ ee and presente d to Grand Lodge at its
next Annual Commun ication for approval or disappro val in the customary fashion provided for the introduc tion of resolutio ns which would
change the law of Grand Lodge.
I strongly urge your support of this recomme ndation. It will provide
for the first time equitable standard s by which all claims for reimburs e-

ment may be judged. As you know, my Brethren , I have endeavored to
encourage the presence of the ladies at many of our functions this year
as well as the participation of the youth organizations and their representatives. Your response to this request has been most gratifying and
I am satisfied that we have been able to provide our families and our
youth organizations with a better understanding of Freemasonry.
On two occasions, therefore, during the past year, I felt it of the
utmost importance that the wives of the Grand Lodge Officers be present.
I therefore authorized the expenditure of approximately $560.00 on one
occasion and approximately $370.00 on a second occasion for reimbursement for these expenses. The Special Finance Study Committee has
agreed with the importance of this concept and provides for this reimbursement as a matter of policy.
Because of changes in the areas of lnspectoral compensation, etc.
it may very well be that the adoption of this Special Finance Study Committee report will occasion some additional cost. I would point out that
only 28% of our Inspectors have requested reimbursement for their
travel and every Grand Master and all of the elective Grand Lodge
Officers have contributed of their own funds on numerous occasions.
I am satisfied that those who wish to continue to do so will find nothing
in this report to force them to do otherwise.
I therefore, again, earnestly and sincerely solicit your support on
behalf of this Special Finance Study Committee.
STU OEN TS

It has been carefully and thoroughly pointed out in the 1967 Proceedings: Report of Special Committee for Programs for Students, that
"the Clubhouses are no longer serving their intended use." The Committee carefully documents the tremendous d ecline in membership and
the change in students' needs. The Clubhouses originally served to find
jobs and housing. These needs are currently met by extensive on-campus
services. The Committee also documented the changing nature of student
activities today. All of the details of this account can be found in the
Committee's report as well as in the references to it by Grand Master
Dayton in his 1967 message. It is understandable that the Directors of
the Clubhouses, w ho have given so much of themselves and of their
time over many years for the young people, should be reluctant to see
these two Clubhouses at Berkeley and Los Angeles sold. However,
Recommenda tion No. 8 of the Grand Master was adopted in 1967 as
follows:
"l. That the incoming Grand M aster appoint a special committee
to formulate plans for the incorporation of a multi-purpose foundation
under the auspices and control of Grand Lodge to establish and administer a flexible program of student aid and submit such plans for approval
at the 1968 Annual Communication.

We are now approaching the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Youth
Organizations. lt seems to me more important than ever that we broaden
our support for these fine groups. The Youth Orders Committee can
serve as a liaison group between our Grand Lodge and the California
Masonic affiliated youth orders. I urge that the committee also devote
careful study to the problem of financial support and human support
and report to Grand Lodge each year the results of their study and recommend legislation based upon that study.
The Y outb Orders Committee has prepared brochures which you will
receive soon after this Communication and which will provide a better
understanding and better communication between Freemasonry and
DeMolay, Job's Daughters and Rainbow for Girls.
Because of my firm conviction that the finest young people in the
land are those involved in DeMolay, Rainbow for Girls and Job's Daughters, I have this year for the first time in the history of our Grand Lodge,
set aside a short period on Tuesday morning of this Communication at
which time the Grand Lodge will be called from labor to refreshment for
the purpose of hearing from the young people who head the respective
organizations.
Gayle Marsh, Grand Worthy Advisor, Rainbow for Girls, is twenty
years old. She graduated from high school in her hometown of Fresno
and will return to her role of college student at Fresno State College
when her year as Grand Worthy Advisor is finished. I understand she
plays the" folk" guitar quite well and considers this an interesting hobby.
Gayle Stiltner, Grand Bethel Honored Queen, Job's Daughters, is
from Richmond. She is a Junior at California State College in Hayward
and is majoring in Psychology. One of her greatest pleasures is reading
and her favorite spectator sport is ice hockey.
Robert W. Laversin, Master Councilor of the Northern California
DeMolay Association, is from San Francisco. He attended San Francisco City College and is now enrolled in California State College at
Hayward where be is majoring in Business Administration. Bob was on
the Varsity Golf Team at George Washington High School and was
an Eagle Scout. He plans to become a Certified Public Accountant.
The administrative duties of the Grand Mas ter in recent yea rs have
grown by leaps and bounds. We are performing almost exactly three
times as many public ceremonies as we were ten years ago. I am satisfied
that these ceremonies present Freemasonry in its most favorable aspect
to the public and that they should be continued. There are increasing
demands upon the Grand Master's time in the various duties appertaining to his office. In order to provide him with invaluable assistance, in

HAWAIIAN VtSITATIO N

One of the most enjoyable highlights of this Masonic year, as it is,
of course, with every Grand Master, began on Saturday June 15th when
we journeyed from our visit to the Annual Communi cation of the Grand
Lodge of Oregon to the Lodges in Hawaii. The hospitality of the State
of Hawaii is known in every corner of the world, but if possible, its
Masonic hospitality is even warmer and more delightful.
On Sunday, June 16 we had the privilege of a ttending services at the
Hawaii Kauaiahau Church where we were introduced to the congregation by the very famous Dr. Akaka, the rector, who delivered an extraordinarily fine sermon. Worshipf ul Howard Wong, the Master of Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, his family, and a group of other Brethren accompan ied
us to that Sunday morning service.
I subsequen tly had the privilege of laying a wreath at the tomb of
the Unknown Soldier at the very famous Punchbow l Cemetery, Pacific
National Monumen t. It was the same morning that the Japanese Prince
had visited and laid a wreath at the same tomb.
Our first ceremony was the Installatio n of Officers of Bethel No. 2
of the Internatio nal Order of Job's Daughters . The ceremony was most
impressive and the young people in attendanc e performed exceeding ly
well.
On my visit to the Hawaiian Lodges I had a luncheon meeting with
three Masonic Brethren who were interested in the formation of a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii. I had requested that our two Inspectors for the area
be invited and they were in attendanc e. Our discussion was most interesting. My concern as has been noted by previous Grand Masters in
their report to this Grand Lodge, was that all of the Brethren be given
an opportuni ty to decide what they regarded as best for Freemaso nry
in the Islands. In reviewing the material presented by the small number
of Brethren interested in forming the Grand Lodge of Hawaii now, I
found the informatio n incomplet e and at times rather misleading . In
discussing the question of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii with many of
the Brethren in the Lodges on all of the Islands, I learned that there were
some who preferred not to ha\'e a Grand Lodge of Hawaii; there were
some who felt that the time was not yet here when it could be successful ly
formed but that there would be a time in the future; and a third group
wished to establish the Grand Lodge of Hawaii as soon as possible.
Because of the interest of the Brethren I have asked the Committe e
which I appointed in response to Recomme ndation No. 2 of Grand
M aster Dayton to prepare factual material concernin g the cost, the needs.
the expectatio ns, etc. and the requireme nts for the formation of a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii. This committee which was to serve "as unbiased consultants to the Lodges in H awaii" is now preparing this material.
The problem in Hawaii is unique and quite different from mainland

California , for many of the members of Hawaiian Lodges live outside
of the state. For example, Ka uai Lodge No. 589 has approxima tely onethird of its membership living on Kauai, one-third living in H onolulu ,
and one-third living in California . I am advised that somewhat similar
conditions prevail in other Hawaiian Lodges.
The official receptions of the various Lodges in Hawaii were memorable events.
On the morning of Ju ne 24th, we were taken by Worshipf ul John
Sun Pui Lau. the Master of Pearl Harbor Lodge No. 598, in the Admiral's gig, to lay a wreath at the U .S.S. Arizona Memorial. It was a
solemn and thought-p rovoking occasion. I could not help but reflect
with sorrow on the supreme sacrifice of these men who had served their
country. I was saddened by the thought that the task to which they
contribute d their lives had not yet been completed .
On Saturday, June 29th we laid the cornerston e of the new Masonic
Temple of Schofield Lodge No. 443. After consultati on with many of
the Past Grand Masters and others, it was decided because of the
unusual nature of the event to have the Deputy Grand Master. the
Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, the Grand Marshal and the Grand
Tiler participate in the ceremony. This they did with great dignity,
reflecting honor on our Grand Lodge. I was presented with a gavel in
the shape of a pineapple which has made a fine addition to an extraor ~
dinary collection of gavels this year. The ingenuity in the fabrication
of these gavels has been so marked tha t I have been tempted many times
to call this the "year of the gavel."
From Honolulu, we visi ted the Lodges on the other islands, Kauai,
Maui and Hawaii. On Kauai, we discovered that the Master of the
Lodge. Worshipf ul Victor Punua was also Master of Ceremonie s for
one of the finest Hawaiian musical groups in the islands. His charming
lady was reported to be the most outstandin g hula dancer and teacher
in H awaii. So enchanted were we by the Hawaiian music and dancing
that we invited the entire group to perform for the Grand Lodge at its
Monday night entertainm ent. I trust that all of you will enjoy them as
much as we did.
It is not possible in words to convey the depth of Masonic feeling
and brotherho od experienc ed in H awaii. I can but assure you, my
Brethren that there is no finer Masonic brotherho od anywhere.
GRAND LODGE APnONS AND COLLARS

In I 965 our Grand Secretary pointed out that the old white velvet
gold trimmed aprons and collars of Grand Lodge had become "disrep~
utable." The set of blue and gold aprons and collars which were purchased in I 964 have become the "traveling set." A second set was
purchased which was used for the first time during the 1965 Annual
Communic ation.

PROCEEDIN GS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNI A

With the greatly increased number of ceremonies requiring the use
of the regalia for the opening of Grand Lodge in various parts of the
Grand Jurisdiction, there should be, I am advised, two traveling sets,
one essentially for the north and one essentially for the south. This
would necessitat e the purchase of a new set of collars and aprons which
could be kept primarily for the Annual Communi cation and for special
use that they might be preserved for a long time, in good condition.

gold aprons and collars, for use by the Grand Lodge officers.
OTHER GRAND JURISDICTI ONS

With the assistance of the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens, the Grand Secretary and the Grand Lecturer.
who on various occasions represente d our Grand Lodge with great
distinction, it was possible for one or another of us to visit the Grand
Lodges of Nevada, Colorado, Oklahoma , Arizona, Indiana, Oregon,
Washingt on, British Columbia and Idaho.
It was my privilege to be invited to give the official response for the
visiting Brethren at the Annual Communi cation of the Grand Lodge of
Colorado in January of 1968. We were met in Denver on January 21st
by our very gracious host, the Most Worshipf ul Charles T. Gore, Grand
Master of Masons in Colorado and his lovely wife. A special visit was
arranged for Mrs. Hopp and me through a new snowfall, to the Air Force
Academy at Colorado Springs. We were met at the Academy by Captain Gerard, a Master Mason, and teacher at the Academy who conducted us on a tour of the classrooms, the various buildings, the magnificent chapel and the hospital. Every citizen can be proud of that extraordinar ily fine Air Force Academy and the facilities provided to the
students. On our visit to the Academy hospital I had the opportuni ty
to "talk shop" with the Command ing Officer.
Our visit to the Grand Lodge of Colorado left memories that will
long be cherished.
The Deputy Grand Master. the Grand Secretary and I attended the
1SOth Anniversa ry Celebratio n of the Grand Lodge of Indiana. Several
years of preparatio n by that Grand Lodge made this one of the most
outstandin g Masonic events of the year. I was particular ly pleased to
note that the incoming Grand Master is a Physician .
We have always had cordial relations with our neighborin g Grand
Jurisdictions, and on the occasion of a reception for the Grand Master
at Truckee, there were present several officers of the Grand Lodge of
Nevada: Robert H . Parker, Past Grand Master; James A. Morrison.
Deputy Grand Master and George M. McTigue, Grand Standard
Bearer.

Knowledg e of our California Masonic Law is communic ated with
great difficulty to prerequisi te bodies. The communic ation of the law is a
nev~r-ending task. This year despite the clear prohibition in our law
agamst the playing of bingo whether it is called bingo or by any other
n~me, and whether or not there is a monetary or other considerat ion paid
directly to play the game, I had to advise a Shrine Potentate and a
Worthy Patron of an Eastern Star Chapter that they were in violation
of the law.
In another instance. a Masonic club used the Masonic emblem, the
S~uare .and. Compass, without permission and solicited advertisin g in
duect v10latton of our law. I believe that a list of all prerequisite bodies
shoul~ be maintaine d at the Grand Lodge office and an outline of the
essent1a~s of Masonic law in the areas most frequently violated should
be provided the heads of these organizati ons each year.

represe~tat1on at the ~oa~d of Education meetings. As a result they
have discovered the vital importanc e of keeping Freemaso ns informed
about the problems confrontin g our public schools.

FIFTY YEAR PINS

In 1928. then Grand Master Will H. Fis her proposed that we "adopt
the delightful custom of a number of our sister jurisdictions and present
to each California Mason who has been a member of one or an~th~r o.~
our Lodges for half a century, an appropriate token of our appreciation.
The Grand Master recommended that the Grand Secretary be authorized
to prepare an appropriate design and to cause a su'.ficient number of gold
buttons to be made therefrom. This recommendatio n was adopted. The
following year, there appears a picture of that design which we know
today, which had been approved by the Grand Master.

emplo~e~ no tool .in its manuf~cture that could not have been used during

LIBRARY

.At .?ur 1967 Annual Communicatio n Grand Lodge approved as its
polJCy the fervent hope that the Temple Board will explore and in due
course develop ways and means of providing library and museum facilities commensurate with our n eeds and our status in the Masonic
World."
I have always been in wholehearted accord with this policy not only

beca~s~ of a deep and abiding love for good books but because of a strong

conv1ctron that our Grand Lodge cannot be complete without a satisfactory repository for the many fine volumes available to it. I envision
further, a place that can be used by students of history in our public
schools, searching for original references or delving into the relationships
between Freemasonry and public history.
Our Temple Board Trustees , in order to prepare for the future library
have recommended a fifty cent per capita. The Trustees will also request approval for the acquisition of additional property which will serve
to protect our beautiful building from intruders on its physical space. I
strongly urge your support for the recommendatio ns of the Temple Board
of Trustees.

PROCLAMATION
PuBuc ScHOOLs WEEK -APRIL 22ND THROUGH 26nr. 1968
Freemasons have supported public education from its very inception
in the American colonies. We recognized that the PUBLIC SCHOOL
IS THE CORNERSTONE OF LIBERTY. It is a proper foundation
stone upon which today's youth will erect an edifice of good government,
human understanding and individual dignity.
The problems of the public schools today are far different from those
of 1920 when then Grand Master Charles Albert Adams founded
Public Schools Week. They cannot be understood or resolved by only
one week of study but we can in one week, arrange for an exchange of
ideas with some of the dedicated teachers and school officials, for the
purpose of sharing those fundamental values of our free enterprise system which made America so strong.
I request every Mason and every Masonic Lodge in California and
Hawaii to participate actively in a Public Schools Program during the
observance of Public Schools Week, April 22nd through 26th, 1968,
which I hereby proclaim.
I direct that no Lodge meetings or rrograms be held during this period except for Public Schools Ob~en-;1nu: with the exception of Stated
Meetings.
This proclamation shall be communicated in each Lodge by one or
more of the following:
] . Read at the March and April Stated Meetings.
2. Mailed to every member of the Lodge.
3. Published in the Lodge Tresdebo<ird.
Dated: February 9, 1968
Sincerely and Fraternally.

EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

EUGENE S. Hopp
Grand Master

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

CHARTER AMENDMENTS

80

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is my honor to present to you, in accordance with Section 150 of
our Code, my eighth annual report as your Grand Secretary.
The Grand Treasurer's report reflects again the recording of all
moneys received and credited to his account. The detail of di~bursements
made by Grand Lodge during the year has been made available to the
Committee on Finance as required by law. Supporting books. papers and
vouchers are on file in the accounting office. All records of a financial
nature have been audited. The certified audits reflecting the records will
be published in the Proceedings. The summarization of consoli?ated ~e­
ceipts and disbursements for the year ending June 30, 1968: mclu?mg
Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes , Endowments and Trust Funds, California Masonic Memorial Temple, bequests, capital gains and others; entails a tremendous volume of paper work. These are carefully segregated
into the appropriate accounts by entity. The convenience and practicability of such a centralized accountin~ program, whic~ has been in effect
throughout the years, continues to be confirmed d~1ly ~hrough the e~se
of handling the increased volume of recording required m the account1~9
office. Efforts continue to be m.:!de to keep abreast of and to practice
proven, modern accounting techniques. Following. prior consultation
with our auditors, certain mechanical improvements m our systems have
been installed and simplifications instituted which have made our accounting more flexible and capable of even greater dema~ds. We have
made much progress and continue to strive for further 1mproveme~ts.
The "team" effort on the part of our constituent Lodge officers, particulady the 711 dedicated Secretaries, the Inspectors'. and ou.r loyal. ~ffice
staff, has made these many accomplishments possible. It is a privilege
to be a part of that team.
