Change of Meeting Place:
Following is a list of Lodges and the changes of meeting place which
have occurred during the year:
Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625 from Playa del Rey to Hawthorne.
Westminster Lodge No. 787 from Seal Beach to Westminster.
Los Altos Lodge No. 712 from Palo Alto to Los Altos.
These changes of meeting place have been officially ap proved under
the authority of the Grand Master, and the Grand Secretary now requests permission to endorse their charters.
(NOTE: Approved. See Reports of Committees on Charters and on
By~Laws for action taken.)
Consolidation of Lodges:
All requirements of the law respect ing consolidation having been
complied with the Grand Secreta ry requests authority to properly
endorse the following charters :
East Bay Lodge No. 489 with H illcrest Lodge No. 573, effective
December 1, 1967, to be known as E ast Bay Lodge No. 489.
Sunrise Lodge No. 522 with Belvedere N o. 539. effective Ju ly 1,
1968, to be known as Belvedere Sunrise Lodge No. 522.
Berkeley Lodge No. 363 with Charter Rock Lodge No. 410. effective
July 1, 1968. to be known as Berkeley Lodge N o. 363.
Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478 with Indian Reck Lodge No. 638,
effective October. I, 1968, to be known as Thousand Oaks Lodge N o.
478.
North Butte Lodge No. 230with Emmanuel Lodge No. 318, effective
October 8. 1968, to be known as North Butte Lodge No. 230.
(NOTE: Approved. See Report of Committee on Charters.)
P ER CA PITA TAX

Palm Desert Lodge U .D. was instituted on May 29, 1968 . This
Lodge collected a less amount of dues than the per capita tax, and in
accord with precedent the Grand M aster. at our suggestion, d irected
that they be not required to pay the per capita tax. It is respectfully
requested that this be approved.
(NOTE: Approved. See Report of Committee on Finance.)
New Lodges
Palm Desert Lodge U.D. , located a t Palm Desert, was formed during
the year. Dispensation granted May 1, 1968. The Lodge was instituted
May 29, 1968, at Palm Desert. Most Worshipful Eugene S. Hopp,
Grand Master, presiding.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF C ALIFORN IA

SOJOURNERS

85

EXHIBIT A

Pursuant to the permission granted at the last Annual Communication to make na mes and addresses of non-resident California members
known to the local Lodges in jurisdictions where they currently reside,
this program was carried out. We have had many favorable comments
with respect to this. As names and addresses of sojourning members
residing in California and Hawaii are received from other jurisdictions.
we sort and forward them to our Lodges nearest their residences. Where
there is concurrent jurisdiction, we follow the same procedttre as is our
custom with Veteran Buttons for sojourning Brethren.
GRAND LODGE LIBRARY

As Grand Librarian, I noted with pleas ure the action taken by the
Grand Lodge at its bst Annual Communication with respect to developing library and museum facilities commensurate with our needs a~d
s tatus in the Masonic world. The foresight of Grand Lodge and its
favorable response to the recommendation made by Past Grand Master
Dayton has been accepted with favor by the membership and has resulted in the receipt of additional books and museum items of historic
importance.
The need for development of such a facility was emphasized to your
Grand Librarian as a result of a visit last year to the Grand Lodge
Library in England; and re-emphasized this year when he visited the
beautiful and outstanding Grand Lodge Library in Cedar Rapids, Iowa.
when returning from the Washington Conferences.
More complete comments will be made on this subject by both the
Board of Library Commissioners and the Trustees of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple during this session.

TRIAL R ECORD No. 1946
A member of Needles Lodge No. 326 was found ~uilty of unMas•:>nk conduct in that he had sexual relations with the wife of a Master Mason. The accused was duly given notice of the ch~rges and failed
to reply. The trial master fixed the penalty at suspension. The procedures appear to be correct.
Your Committee, however, feels that the accus~d ~as violated a~
important precept of our Fraternity and after considering all the ~vi­
dence in the record is of the opinion that the penalty should be raised
to expulsion. We off er the following resolution:
.
.
.
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilt by the trial master m T~1al
Record No. 19-i6 be approved, but the penalty be raised to ex~~ls1on
and that the accused be expelled from all of the rights and pnv1leges
of Masonry.
Adopted.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
It is the duty of the Grand Lecturer, according to the California
Masonic Code, to render to the Grand Lodge at each Annual Communication a full and detailed account of his services during the year, and
to set forth therein a report of the condition of the Lodges throughout
the jurisdiction. This report . accordingly, will cover the various activities
and responsibilities attendant upon those duties prescribed in the Code.
However, because of the structure of activities under the Grand Lecturer's direction, this report will also include various activities of the
Ritual Committee and the lnspectoral Corps.
RITUA L

Our Ritual is the lifeblood of Freemasonry in California, and it
serves as a vehicle by which the duties of Freemasonry are imparted to
our candidates. It is our Ritual and the manner in which it is employed
to teach our candidates that has elevated and maintained Freemasonry
preeminent among fraternal organizations. Our Grand Lodge, since its
inception, has long recognized the importance of striving for uniformity
in the work and conformity among the constituent Lodges. Consequently, a system of instructions has been developed over the past 35
years whereby our adopted Ritual is taught by the Grand Lecturer and
the Ritual Committee, through the Inspectoral Corps, to the constituent
Lodges and brethren. There is ample evidence that our present system
is achieving the desired results. The following activities were directed
toward this end.
I. The annual review of our adopted Ritual by the Ritual Committee was held at San Luis Obispo on December 1-3, 1967, under the direction of the Grand Lecturer.
2. The Division Conferences for the Inspectors were conducted by
the Assistant Grand Lecturers as follows, with all members of the Ritual
Committee present :
Division One at Concord, April 19-21, 1968, conducted by Worshipful Bertram von Konsky, Assistant Grand Lecturer;
Division Two at Bijou, June 21-23, 1968, conducted by Worshipful
Frank P . Lemen , Assistant Grand Lecturer;
Division Three at Carmel. May 3-5, 1968, conducted by Worshipful
Ulysses Patropulos, Assistant Grand Lecturer;
D ivision Four at Cambria, June 7-9 . 1968, conducted by Worshipful
Wallace H. Fiske;
Division Five at San Diego. May 17-19, 1968, conducted by Worshipful Burton Meyer, Jr.;
Division Six at Oceanside, March 29-31 , 1968, conducted by Worshipful William H. Price.

3. Each Assistant Grand Lecturer conducted four to nine Schools
of Instruction for the Inspectors in the r~spective Divisions.
4. The Grand Lecturer's School of Instruction for Inspectors was
conducted on Saturday, October 12, 1968, as prescribed in the California
Masonic Code.
5. The Inspectors of the various Districts conducted Schools of Instruction for the officers of their respective Districts. The total of these
Schools in the various Districts averaged approximately seven per District.
6. In addition to the foregoing chain of instruction, the Masters and
Officers' Coaches of the constituent Lodges held and conducted Schools
of Instruction and rehearsals for the Officers of the individual Lodges.
Throughout the jurisdiction, the individual Lodges averaged fourteen
such Schools and rehearsals during the year.
Our steady progress for uniformity in our work and conformity to
our adopted Ritual is evidenced by the increasing proficiency exemplified
by the Inspectors at the various Division Conferences and at the Grand
Lecturer's School of Instruction. Further. the Inspectors' reports on the
work of the Officers in the various Districts indicates progress toward
greater proficiency among the Officers of the constituent Lodges.
By direction of your Grand Lecturer, Assistant Grand Lecturer
Wallace H. Fiske conducted a School of Instruction for the Inspectors
and Officers' Coache5 in the State of Hawaii. This program of instruction, adopted a few years ago, continues to show excellent results, and
provides ample evidence that our brethren in Hawaii continue to join
us in striving for perfection.
CANDIDATE'S COACHING

When the Candidate's Coaching program was instituted in 1962,
with the Handbook for Candidates' Coaches developed as an integral
part of the program, it was recommended by the then Grand Lecturer
Donald G . Campbell that the Senior Wardens in the constituent Lodges
be put in charge of the Candidate Coaching program. It is recognized
that this was merely a Tecommendation, and that it was not mandatory.
to permit flexibility. However, our most recent records indicate that a
total of 156 Districts of our 184 Districts have adopted the recommended
program and put it into effect. There are indications that this delegation
of authority to the Senior Warden has been most beneficial to this par~
ticular program.
One of the basic features of the Candidate' s Coaching program was
through the use of the Handbook for Candidates' Coaches to provide
an individual Coach with pertinent information and knowledge of Freemasonry to impart to the Candidate during his coaching periods. It was
anticipated that in this manner our candidates would become more fully

Candidate's Coaches would study and become familiar with the contents of the Handbook and thus qualif.y for certification by the Inspector

Coaching. Further, that the various Masters, in ·c ooperation with the

LooGE Acr1v1rrns

The great majority of the Inspectors' annual reports indicate that the
Lodges are filling the needs of the community, and that M asonry is advancing in the Districts.
Practically all Lodges are reported as having participated in or conducted an observance of our Grand Lodge Public Schools Week program, Constitution Observance, and promoted our Homes Endowment
Program. These activities. of course, will be reported on more fully by
the various Grand Lodge Committees involved.
However, some of our Lodges are encounterin g problems in regard
to both growth a nd activity. M any of our rural Lodges particularly are
beset with declining membership s, principally because the younger men
of the community are moving to other locations, leaving the Past Masters in many instances to carry on the activities of the Lodge. Also there
are Lodges located in metropolitan areas wherein the Temples are in
deteriorating areas of the city, and thus are not attracting new members.
Further, there are a few Lodges that are beset with factionalism and
dissension within their ranks, thus preventing growth and a ctivity. In
addition, some Lodges are handicapped by ineffective leadership, and
indifference on the part of the membership .
The foregoin g is evidenced in the Inspectors' annual reports whe-rein
47 Inspectors have indicated that the Lodges in their Districts have difficulty in obtaining adequate officer material, reasons being lack of interest, devotion to family ties, prior commitment s, and unwillingne ss to
devote the time necessary. This is further evidenced by the fact that
approximate ly 10% of our Masters serving this year are Past M as ters,
8 % of our Senior Wardens are Past Masters, a nd 8% of our Junior
Wardens are Past Masters.

CONCERN S

l. Funeral Service -We continue to receive criticism of the manner
in which our Funeral Service is being performe d in some areas of our
jurisdicti on. The Funeral Service is the means by which the uninitiat ed
and the general public are exposed to and form an impressi on of Freemasonry in general. and we must determin e that such impressi ons and
attitudes are in keeping with the stature and purposes of our fraternit y.
While it is true that certain sections of the Code imply that any Master Mason may perform the ceremon y, it is equally true that the Funeral
Service is Ritual. and therefore under the direction and control of the
Grand Lecturer and Ritual Committ ee, and conseque ntly in turn falls
under the direction of the Inspecto r to see that all Ritual is properly
performe d. Therefor e. following preceden ts of Grand Lecturer s Chester H. Warlow and Elbert W . Davis. who issued directive s for the purpose of tightenin g up the. control of our Funeral Service rendition s, we
are presently working out details of a program calculate d to insure that
our Funeral Service is properly performe d in the various areas of our
jurisdicti on by Master Masons who have demonst rated their proficiency.
2. Degree Teams- It has come to our attention that Degree Teams
compose d of brothers holding members hip in related organiza tions or
occupati onal groups are conferrin g degrees in our Lodges, with the consent of the Masters. devoid of the dignity and profkie.n cy required of
our Lodge officers. The. policy of the Ritual Committ ee. establish ed in
1955. provides that no Degree Team shall be invited by the Master to
confer a degree or any portion thereof unless the Master has, through
the Inspecto r of his District, received assuranc e as to the proficien cy of
the respectiv e members of the Degree Team in the stations or places
they are to occupy in the degree.
We cannot permit, in our Lodges, the kind of work which is marred
by poor rendition of the Ritual. Therefor e, we Insist that the Masters
of the various lodges. and the Inspecto rs, wherein such Degree Te.ams
are utilized, strictly comply to the policy heretofore. stated.

In previous reports. it has been expresse d that an Inspecto r's Manual. for guidance of all Inspecto rs, particula rly the newly appointe d.
was highly desirable . Much thought and consider ation has been directed
toward this end, and during this year consider able progress has been
made toward the ultimate compilat ion of the material deemed to be pertinent to such a handboo k of informat ion. The help and cooperat ion of
our Grand Master, Most Worship ful Eugene S. Hopp, in working out
details is particula rly apprecia ted.
The status of the proposed Manual is that the ultimate content has
been generally determin ed, the material assemble d under various categories. and is now in the process of indexing . It is expected that it w ill
soon be complete d, edited, reproduc ed. and ready for distribut ion to the
Inspecto rs.

CONCLUS ION

Another year of service approach es its end. and in consider ing our

REPOR T OF THE TRUST EES OF THE
MASON IC HOME S
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Masonic Homes of Californ ia located at Union City and Covina
are the outstand ing example s of Californ ia Masonry in practice. They
are the embodim ent of the principle s of Masonic assistanc e to those in

110

111

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFO RNIA

need. E very Mason can be justly proud of this practical exemplifkation
of our Masonic teachings and philosophy. As required by the Masonic
Code, the Board herewith makes its Annual Report and. sta tistically. it
constitutes the 76th report so made by the Board.
The work required of the Trustees is extremely heavy. The entire
Board meets every month , alternating the meeting place monthly between
San Francisco and Los Angeles. Each Trustee, prior to the meeting.
receives a summary of every application for admission and the investigator's report in connection with the application. In addition to the
Co;lsideration of each application. the Board must give attention to the
financial requirements necessary to maintain the Homes as outstanding
institutions. All of these matters require many hours of hard and ardous
work by each and every Trustee. The author of this report is the President of the M asonic Homes of California and, while the report is concurred in by all of the Trustees. he desires to pay tribute to the unselfish
devotion of each and every Trustee and to the long hours of labor contributed during the present year to Board matters.
Our Masonic law provides for three Trus tees ex officio. the Deputy
Grand Master, the Senior Grand Warden and the Junior Grand Warden . The other six Trustees are appointed by successive Grand Masters.
three being resiclents in the vicinity of the Home at Union City, and
three being residents in the vicini ty of the Home at Covina. Under
Masonic law, the Grand Treasurer is the Treasurer of the Homes and
the Grand Secretary is the Secretary of the Board of Trustees and of
the Homes. \ V hen the Board met immediately after the close of the
Annual Communication in 1967, for the purpose of organizing. the
election of Robert A. Crigler as Deputy Grand Master, Chester R.
MacPhee as Senior Grand Warden, and Herbert A. Huebner as Junior
Grand Warden. was reported to the Board. There w:is also reported to
the Board the appointment by Grand Master Eugene S. Hopp of Myron
E. Smith and Lau rence E. D<lyton for a three-year term each. and on
motion the ex officio designees and the appointed Trustees were elected
as members of the Board. Phil N . Myers and Donald G. Campbell.
whose terms expire in 1968. and Alfred F. Breslauer and Edward J.
Blickfeldt. whose terms expire in 1969. constitute the remaining members of the Board.
The Board proceeded with the election of the Officers of the Board.
Alfred F. Breslauer was elected President of the Board and Donald G.
Campbell was elected Vice President. As sta ted before. the GranJ
Treasurer. Paul A. Pflueger. and the Grand Secretary, Edward H.
Siems. constituted the Treasurer and the Secretary of the Board.
There is attached to this report a detailed report of the Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Union City, Gail H. David, and the
report of the Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Covina. James
C . Blain e. The Board. as well as the entire fraternity. owes great appre~

ciation for their fine work as evidenced by these reports, and for their
efficient administration.
What have been the significant changes during the year 1968 which
should be reported by the Board? Perhaps the most significant change
was in connection with the admission policies for the Home at Union
City regarding non-ambulatory applicants. Written notice of this change
was given to the Masters of the Constituent Lodges. and we will here
paraphrase such notice. Our Board has for some time been deeply concerned over the fact that a number of applicants for the Home at Decoto
could not be admitted because of their physical condition. This was
primarily for the reason that the Home has been licensed by the State
Department of Public Welfare for a mbulatory residents only. In other
words, one who could not take care of his personal needs without help
and who would not be able to leave the building quickly without assistance in emergencies could not be accepted as a resident in the Home.
Needless to say, this policy gave much concern to the Lodges themselves. because inability to accept an applicant in many of these cases
caused some discontent within the Lodge.
After a thorough review of the situation with representatives 0f the
Welfare Department and the State F ire Marshall, it has been determined that the third and fourth floors of Adams H all could be licensed
for non-ambulatory residents by making certain minor adjustments not
in\'olving structural change. The Board took the necessary steps and an
application wns made to the Department of Social Welfare for nonambulatory applicapts. The renewal of the license for the Home at
Union City included limited provisions for non-ambulatory applicants.
This will mean that it will be possible in the future to accept a limited
number of applicants who require more care and supervision than is
permissible in facilities restricted to the ambulatory. This will mean, for
example, that we could take in a husband and wife where one is ambulatory and the other is not.
Let me point out specifically. however, that those who require pro~
fessional care (nursing home or hospital cases) will continue to be
ineligible for admission. It is important that the Lodges clearly under~
stand that nursing home or hospital care cases cannot be accepted. We
feel that the Lodge, before filing a n application, should be certain that
the <:1pplicant is not a nurs ing home or hospital case, so that neither the
applica nt nor the Lodge will be disappointed when such an application
cannot be accepted for admission. The hospital maintained at Union
City is only for such cases as arise when admitted applicants subse~
quently require professional nursing care or assistance. The license
from the Department of Social Welfare was effective from July 15,
1968, and applications from and after that date will be considered under

the expande d license. The applicati on form has been modified and supplementa ry instructi ons will accompa ny the applicati on form.

should arise.
During the past year, another innovatio n in connection with the
operatio n of the Board was the appointm ent of one of our Trustees .
Laurence E. D ayton, on a retainer basis as counsel for the Homes. The
regular business of the Boa rd has increased immeasu rably over the past
several years. including additiona l estates in which the Homes Board
has been named as beneficia ry and the Board felt that it was time to
obtain a designat ed counsel. even though it were on a part-time basis.
Brother Dayton is an accompli shed attorney and during the year has
discharg ed his duties in a most creditabl e manner.
It was during the past year. also, that progress was made on a
matter that has been pending a number of years . The descripti on by
which the real property at Union City was acquired . which was a number of years ago. was vague and uncertain , and referred to some landmarks difficult to locate. Since its acquisiti on. the property has greatly
increased in value. A survey o f the property was complete d and legal
action has been filed to establish the boundar y lines as fixed by the
survey as the boundar y lines of the property . At the las t session of
Grand Lodge. certain legislatio n was adopted to clear up the transmit tal
of title to the property from the former Trus tees to the present corporation. the Masonic Homes of Californ ia. When the pending litigation is
complete d, the title w ill be fully establish ed in Masonic Homes of California to all of the property covered by the survey,
With reference to the Home at Covina. the past year witnesse d the
introduc tion of several new programs. One of these. a compreh ensive
vocation al testing program , has been impleme nted in a practical way.
We have vocation al contacts with members of the Craft in the special
field in w hich the particula r child has shown some aptitude. The interest
of the Fraterni ty. as always. is not only for the period during which
the child resides at Covina, but also in whateve r business, profession or
employm ent such child pursues after residenc e at the Home.

In the de-escala tion of the farm and animal project at the Home , the
general barn, farm and animal area has been changed into a recreatio nal
and vocation al site. The Superint endent's report shows in detail what
changes are contemp lated and what changes are being made. We are
most grateful to members of the Craft who have donated generous ly of
their time and effort in connecit on with the foregoin g and other activities
at the Home.
It appears that no chan ge will be made in the location of the Children's Home. and that it will remain at Covina. Refurbis hing and repairs
have been made on the present buildings. but ultimatel y it will be necessary for some new structure s to be erected. During this past year the
first steps have been taken for such master redevelo pment. The initial
step of interview ing responsi ble architect s and planning firms has been
undertak en and the Board will continue with its usual careful attention
to this project.
The recreatio nal facility at Big Bear has been improved during the
year and represen ts a valuable asset in the Homes' list of propertie s.
In line with all business activities . the Board has had to face the
increased cost of materials and increased wages. As yet, there is no
indicatio n that the coming year will reflect any reduction in these items.
However . it is the consider ed opinion of the Board of Trustees that the
Homes will be able to operate upon a lower per capita tax than last year
and the Board is requestin g the sum of $1.15 as a per capita tax. The
reason for this action of the Board is due primarily to a number of fac~
tors, namely. the increase of our Endowm ent Fund and other reserve
funds. the ability-o f the Investme nt Committ ee to obtain a good percentage return upon the investme nts of the Homes . decrease d medical
costs by reason of Medicar e. and the substant ial increase in the number
of bequests which the Homes recei ved during the past year.
This leads to the concludi ng statemen t of my report, of our great
apprecia tion to those who have so remembe red the Homes and have
provided for them in their w ill. This report is closed , also. with gratitude
to all of the employe es for their diligence during the year. to our Grand
Secretar y and to our Grand Treasure r for their untirin g efforts, a nd to all
who have made the Masonic H omes of Californ ia the Grea t Light of
Masonic accompli shment.

REPOR T OF SUPER INTEN DENT- COVIN A HOME
It is with pleasure that I submit my third Annual Report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina. At the year's end
our populatio n consisted of sixty-six children with twenty-s ix girls and
forty boys. Element ary enrollees numbere d thirty, Junior High eighteen .
::ind Senior High eighteen . June 1968 saw two young men graduate .
Wilson Perkins. Sojourne r Lodge No. 607, will be attending Automot ive
Mechani c School in Septemb er 1968, and William Cooper, Eden Lodge
No. 113, who will be enrolling at Azusa Pacific College as a Liberal
Arts Major.
Septemb er I 0. 1967 saw our Covina Home rededirn ted by Grand
Master Dayton, "Pete" Anderso n. Presiden t of the Board, the Board
of Trustees , and approxim ately 700 visitors and guests.
Our Home family has enjoyed relatively good health, for which we
are grateful. Customa ry colds. scratches and an occasional stitch helped
keep the infirmary partially occupied .
Many changes have taken place at Covina. A compreh ensive Vocational Testing program has been started. Follow-u p vocation al contacts have been arranged for our children with members of the Craft.
These contacts serve to answer question s, give counsel. guidance , and
share knowled ge with the children about selected professio ns, job responsibilities. opportun ities for advancem ent. etc.
The general barn , farm and animal area of the Home is in process
of being converte d into a Recreati onal-Voc ational site. Animal stalls
have been removed from the barn and this are.a converte d into an indoor
recreatio n building. Feeding pens have been removed , paved , and are
in process of conversi on to basketba ll, volleyba ll, and badminto n courts.
Farrowin g pens are in process of conversi on to bicycle repair, basic wood
shop. lapidary, and simple automoti ve repairs. PBX and secretari al experience is also being offered. These activities have been planned as a
result of the Vocation al Testing program referred to above.
Surveyin g. layout, specifications, and engineer ing for this project
were all complete d by voluntee rs within our Fraternit y. Bids for renovation were received from six firms with the low bid being awarded to
a member of the Craft.
At year's end. three couples were serving as Housepa rents for three
groups of children, affording them an opportun ity to be more "family
centered ." The feeling of fa mily was manifest ed when one couple left
for the hospital so that the Housemo ther could have her baby and seven
teen age boys wanted to go along to "greet their new baby."
Many contribut ions and gifts have been received from individua ls
and groups- not the least of which have been gifts by members of De.-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFOR N IA

117

Malay, Job's Daughte rs, and Rainbow Girls . Special thanks go to the
"Jo-De~Ra's" from San Francisc o who as a result o f their annual variety
show presente d our children with a beautiful Motion Picture Projecto r
and Screen.
Our Masonic H ome Alumni were quite active. A picnic and two
dinner-d ances were held and ma ny childhoo d memories were shared.
Many other alumni stopped by to say "hello" and also show their chi!~
dren where they lived their early years.
Our children have been involved in many and varied supervise d
activities. Weeken d and residenti al camping . special educatio nal and
cultural trips. music lessons, ballet. self-defe nse courses are popular and
participa tion encourag ed. F our young men are active in DeMola y.
Scouting and Campfi re occupy the spare time of some. All children
have savings accounts and are proud of them. All dorms have their
service projects, and all children look forward to your visits.
We again extend to our many friends an invitation to visit Covina
when time permits. We are grateful to the Board of Trustees and the
Masons of Californ ia and Hawaii for their continue d interest and support. Our children thank you.
Respectf ully submitte d,

ANNU AL REPOR T OF THE
MASON IC HOMES ENDOW MENT BOARD
The members of the Homes Endowm ent Board take pleasure in presenting to you their report for the year ending June 30. 1968.
During the past year. with the assistanc e of Worshipful George
Calderwood of Long Bench Lodge No. 327, Worship ful Don Ingalls of
North Hollywo od Lodge No. 542, and Brother Lowell Keeley of Burbank Lodge No. 406 (and Walt Disney Studios) . we develope d and
presented 110 times a narra ted slide program about our two Homes.
Our sincere thanks go to the members of the Board of Trustees w ho supported our efforts in this program and provided the necessar y funds.
The Endowm ent Board members also appeared 265 times before
other groups w here the slides were not shown. All in a ll, we spoke
before lodges or other groups of M asons 375 times . speaking to over
22,500 Masons.
The slide program is good and is now offered for showing in your
lodge. Call or write to the Board member in your area soon. and set a
date fo r a showing to your members and, if possible, their families - it
will help .
The income from the Endowm ent Fund for the past year was
$813.776.35. This has been trans ferred to the operatin g account o f the

Homes. The income continues to grow because of the sincere interest
of the Masons of California in their Homes.

$337,100.65 from gifts or bequests; $19.776.63 from memorials; and
$7.696.83 from donations from organizations and individuals, for a grand

CONCLUSION

"Brotherly Love"-1 feel I have learned of this, this year-every
member of the Board hase given of himself far more than has been asked.
To each of them I give my thanks. To the Grand Master and his officers
who have done so much for our Homes, my gratitude for your leadership and direction.
R io Hondo Lodge No. 800 and its Endowment Chairman have, for a
number of years. worked with a dedicated devotion for our Homes. and
this year top the list of lodges with the largest average contribution per
member. Our sincere thanks to you for this effort.
To the Inspectors: Masters, Wardens and members of the lodges
it is to you we tip our hats. Because of your love of Masonry and your
belief in its te:!chings. our Homes grow strong.
Respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
The Board of Con trol herewith submits the annual report covering
the activities of the twenty Boards of Relief in the various areas of this
jurisdiction. The duties o f the secretaries of these twenty Boards of
Relief involve many requests from other jurisdictions relating to their
sojourning Brethren and families. The duties which our secretaries of
these Boards of Relief perform are many-such as conducting funerals.
calling upon the sick, extending relief, investiga tions and many other
Eunctions too numerous to go into detail.
During the 1967- 1968 Masonic year, the Boards of Relief. through
their executive secretaries and executive committees, have performed
the following functions.
Advanced for relief.............................................. $15,063.79

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This is the Fourteenth Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of
California Masonic Memorial Temple.
At the close of the 1967 Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge, the California Masonic Memorial Temple Trustees met in
Annual Meeting. The President, Ralph H. Head. reported the election
of Robert A . Crigler as Deputy Grand Master, Chester R. MacPhee
as Senior Grand Warden, and Herbert A. Huebner as Junior Grand
Warden. On proper motion they were dul'Y elected members of the
Board of Trustees as provided in the California Masonic Code.
The Board then proceeded to organize with Ralph H. Head as
President, Samuel I. Jacobs as Vice President, Paul A. Pflueger, Grand
Treasurer. as Treasurer, and Edward H. Siems. Past Grand Master
and Grand Secretary, as Secretary.
The terms of the appointed members of the Board were as follows:
Expiring in 1968. Lyle E. Patton and Ralph H. Head; expiring in 1969,
Frank F. Goodman and Carl U. Zachrisson; expiring in 1970, Samuel
I. Jacobs and Howard H. McKinley.
Out in the Black Hills of South Dakota on Mount Rushmore are
carved in bold relief the figures of four great presidents of the United
States, George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln and
Theodore Roosevelt. As you stand below and gaze up at this splendor
in the sky you cannot help but say, "Would that I had been so inspired
as the sculptor to do this great work." But when you learn all of the
history you find that the sculptor did not do it all. He drew the design
on the trestle board and then ordinary workmen with chisel and hammer
in hand did the actual work on the mountainside.
The financial statement of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
for the year ending June 30, 1968, which by reference is a part of this
Report, clearly demonstrates who built this great Temple on Nob Hill
in the City by the Golden Gate: the Masons of California who contributed more than $6.250.000 for its erection.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

147

Because of the fine custodial and business acumen of the Manager
of the Temple. George D. Gavin, income from all sources during the
past fiscal year reached an all-time high of $229,000. After making its
·second annual contribution to the Masonic Homes of California in the
sum of $10,000, the net operating loss for the year was $6,715, or $342
less than the previous year. The financial statement also shows that
$63.000 for depreciation and replacement was added to a reserve fund
now totaling $640,000 or nearly 11 % of the original cost of the building
and furnishings.
In his message to the Grand Lodge at its 1967 Communication, Most
Worshipful Laurence E. Dayton urged the Temple Board to explore
and, in due course, develop ways and means of providing library and
museum facilities which would be commensurate with California's status
in the Masonic world.
Therefore, in keeping with the spirit of Past Grand Master Dayton's recommendation, the Board of Trustees has resolved that Grand
Lodge approve an annual per capita tax of flfty cents per member to
create a reserve fund for the development of an appropriate library and
museum. It is further resolved that plans and costs be submitted to the
Grand Lodge for approval prior to the commencement of construction.
The Trustees cannot urge too strongly the adoption of the resolution. A journey of a 1000 miles must start with one step. A navigator
may study a map for an indeterminable period of time but he will never
be one foot closer to his next destination until he makes a move. Nothing
could be more in keeping with the philosophy and the direction of California Freemasonry than the creation of a library and museum for the
preservation of the records and history of the Grand Lodge, its artifacts,
and the accumulated written knowledge of the ages
The first library in the history of the world was established 4000
years ago in Babylon. In 1698 the first library in America was built in
Charleston, South Carolina. At the instigation of Thomas Jefferson,
the Library of Congress was founded in 1800. Many years ago the
Grand Lodge of Iowa started what is now regarded as the finest
Masonic library in the United States.
Your Trustees believe the time is now at hand for the Masons of
California to take the first step toward the creation of what may well
become the depository of the finest collection of Masonic information
history and memorabilia in the world.
'
There is no more appropriate place and time for that action to be
taken than here and now.
California Masonic Memorial Temple has become the setting and
the showplace for business and professional meetings, for exhibits of
the products of industry. and for concerts. lectures. and premier performan ces. It is the focus of attention of thousands of visitors to San

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully submits its report
for the past year. A review of the activities of the Committee during this
period indicates continuing progress in the construction, maintenance
and operation of Masonic Temple properties. This increasing progress
is reflected in the annual financial statements submitted by the Lodges
and Masonic Temple Associations relative to their financial transactions
and other matters relating to Masonic Temple construction, mainte~
nance and operation. During the past year 310 Temple Associations and
Lodges have submitted financial statements, as required by Section 200
of the Masonic Code. These statements reveal that each year- more and
more interest is being taken in the proper efficient business and .financial
affairs of the Lodges, and as a result, with few exceptions, they are
being operated on a firm . sound financial basis. Each year more Lodges
and Temple Associations are establishing cash and depreciation reserves
which are so important and necessary for the repair, rehabilitation and
replacement of the Temples that will be required in the future.
The increasing and continuing success of the financial operations of
the Temples gives cause for the Committee to again recommend to the
Lodges (who have not done so) that they form non-profit Temple A ssociations to carry on the business and financial matters of their Temples.
During the past year the Committee acted upon approximately 77
applications relating to the purchase of property, the construction of
new Temples, the ·remodeling, repairing and other necessary matters
relating to the financial requirements and operation of Masonic Lodge
facilities. Full details of all the transactions are contained in the Grand
Lodge files. These transactions, together with other miscellaneous re.
quests, required necessary action of the Committee in approximately
110 proceedings. More than 50 visitations were made to various Lodges
to advise and counsel with the brethren concerning problems respecting
Lodge and Temple Association affairs. These visitations, made upon
invitation of the brethren, were in all instances very s uccessful and the
problems satisfactorily resolved.
The Committee again points out the importance of keeping the Temples in proper order and repair. An unpainted, neglected, rundown Tem·
pie creates a very poor image of our fraternity in the community in
which it is located. It is the obligation of the brethren not only to provide
adequate, comfortable and presentable facilities for all who have the
privilege of using the Lodges, but also the obligation to keep pace with
the growth of the community. A well-ordered Temple, indicating good
housekeeping and pride will gain and retain the respect and high regard
of all who view it.

The Committ ee wishes to commend the various Lodges and Temple
Associat ions for their interest and cooperat ion in all matters relating to

The Committ ee again recommends that constant review be made of
insuranc e program s of the Lodges in order to determin e that they are
properly insured in all requirem ents necessar y to protect their property
and their members.

"Our American Constitutional System works only so long as, and
just to the extent that . people believe in it. Our Constitutional government is based upon the belief that future generations will be wise enough
and honest enough and courageous enough to manage their own affairs
without having to be inflexibly bound by the ideas of this or any earlier
period in history. and yet without ever being able to ignore any of the
lessons of history."
Unfortunately. as in the past, too many excellent programs were
presented to sparse audiences. An analysis of the reports submitted by
the Masters would seem to indicate that one answer to the attendance
problem is increased publicity. Another answer. it is still the Committee's thought, is to present a program to an audience already gathered
for another purpose. In connection with this concept, your Committee
contacted the various schools in the State College System. and in a
number of instances we are pleased to report that the schools indicated
a willingness to dedicate a portion of a half-time ceremony at a September football game to the theme of Constitution Observance. Through
this means and through increased attendance at a number of programs
throughout the State, your Committee hopes that it has carried the word
to a greater number of the citizens of California and Hawaii. recognizing
at the same time that we have but taken a short step on a long path. With
the philosophy that any goal worth reaching is worth working toward,
your Committee trusts that each year will see an increased effort on the
part of the Masters and Brethren of the Lodges in our jurisdiction with
the result that each year will likewise bring increased participation and
greater results.
This report would not be complete without a word of thanks to the
Grand Secretary and his staff for their fine assistance. as well as to the
Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden, and
Junior Grand Warden for their enthusiastic support and leadership.

If this year's efforts of the Constitution Observance Committee have
found favor with this Grand Lodge, your Committee asks for no credit
-but, rather, credit should be given for any successes to the Masters.
to their Constitution Observance Committees and to those Masons
themselves whose interest and support are so clearly illustrated by their
participation in the planning and presentation of the many programs
held throughout the jurisdiction. As before, your Committee extends
its heartiest congratulations to those Lodges who have fulfilled their
duties in actively participating in an appropriate Constitution Observance Program, and a ssures the incoming Masters that this Committee

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
At the 1967 Communication all Lodges under dispensation were
~ra~ted charters so there were no carry~overs. Palm Desert Lodge was
instituted May 29th and has applied for a charter.
The Committee met with representatives of the Lodge and examined
t~e records. M inor changes and corrections were suggested. The activities of the Lodge had been somewhat limited during the summer season
but regular meetings were held each week and two candidates received
all three degrees. The finances of the Lodge are in order and there is no
indebtedness.
It is the unanimous recommendation of the Committee that a charter
be gra~ted and number assigned to Palm Desert Lodge-No. 826--in
the unmcorporated community of Palm Desert in the County of Riverside.
During the past year the Committee has studied the membership
records of the past few years and has found that a considerable portion
of new m~mbers of California Masonry, both by degree and affiliation.
has been m Lodges newly formed during this period. We are convinced
tha.t t~ere are still many areas in the State where new Lodges are needed.
This includes new, rapidly growing areas, as well as older areas where
present Lodges have large memberships.
We mention this in our report because we feel that some members
of this Grand Lodge ~ay be aware of such areas and be willing to under~ake t~e task of startmg new Lodges. Information on the steps necessary
is available from the Grand Secretary's office. The Committee on Charters stands rea?y to assist in any manner desired by the Grand Master.
The following consolidations have been referred to this Committee :

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worsh ipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The within report is submitted covering the stewardship of the Committee for the fiscal yearof 1967-1968.
.
There are approximately 129 Masonic Jurisdictions wh1~h ar~ r~c­
ognized by the California Grand Lodge. including 48 Masonic Junsd1c~
tions in the United States.
.
.
All reviews are submitted to the Editorial Staff of the California
Freemason for publication in its quarterly reports.
All reviews cannot be published in the California Freemason as
available space does not permit the publication of all such reviews.
your Committee is a working committee and each member has done
his part during the Masonic fiscal year 1967~1968 in reviewing the proceedings of Masonic Jurisdictions of the United States. S~ace does n~t
permit publishing reviews of proceedings outside the United St~tes m
the California Freemason. During the year Brother Ralph Merriam, a
valued member of the Committee, passed away.
We have followed the style used in our reports of recent years. as
disclosed by the reviews published in the California Freemason in its
quarterly issues.
.
. . .
Editorial comment is minimized and 1s placed m italics. All other
matter is printed without quotation marks, its source being clearly indicated.

GRA N D LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

171

The greatest problem with which we have had to deal has been to
reduce the great amount of available material as contained in the annual
proceedings of foreign jurisdictions to a usable length. So much is happening in the Masonic World that if we quoted everything of interes t.
the reviews would be too long. For this reason, much that is of interest
and truly inspirational has had to be left out.
We have at all times kept in mind the traditional function of the
Correspondence Committee. which is to inform the members of our
Grand Lodge what is being done in sister jurisdictions to further the
interests of Masonry. In this way they may be better informed and
prepared to do their part in reaching intelligent decisions. wherever
possible. for the Grand Lodge of California.
We have reviewed some forty-eight Masonic Jurisdic tions, not including California, but including the District of Columbia . The last two
sta tes admitted as states of the United States. to-wit: Hawaii and
Alaska, are members of the Grand Jurisdictions of California and Washington respectively, and their articles are a part of such jurisdictions.
Various jurisdictions are making a sincere effort to build and solidify
the members' interest in the Fraternity. particularly with newly ra ised
candidates.
California Freemason is referred to on many occasions in reports of
foreign jurisdictions and it has continued to maintain a high standard
of Masonic leadership among publications of like kind among the 48
Grand Jurisdictions of the United States.
The problems of the various jurisdictions as revealed by these reports are quite similar to those which prevail in California. It can be
safely stated that according to these jurisdictions the primary function of a Masonic Lodge, indeed, the primary function of our craft. is
to train its members to a better understanding of the truths which its
rituals and its ceremonies are calculated to inculcate, to develop its members as good citizens, to cultivate social virtues and propagate the teachings of the craft. Every lodge should be concerned with its welfare, the
happiness and development of its members.
We welcome constructive suggestions so that we can, wherever
possible, improve the reviews of other jurisdictions.
A request is hereby made that for the ensuing Masonic year. a budget
of $ 150.00 be allowed to the Committee to take care of its expenses. The
greater portion of the requested budget represents charges by the Cali~
fornia Grand Lodge for expenses entailed in mailing of proceedings
of foreign jurisdictions to the Committee.
Respectfully submitted.
GEORGE W . BURCH, JR., Chairman

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTE E
ON MASONIC EDUCATIO N

publications. I am certain that you will find many subjects of particular
interest to you and to the membership of your Lodge.
Your Chairman would like to share with you two interesting Masonic
educational endeavors which might well be just the type of activity
which would be ideal for your Lodge. In the far north of our jurisdiction,
this C ommittee is represented by Brother John Bowersox, Master of
Humboldt Lodge No. 79, who reports to us of a district educational
meeting which was tried for the first time in this area. The lodges of the
1OOth Masonic District assembled for a no-host dinner attended by new
Master Masons raised during the past year, the coaches and the lodge
officers. Following dinner the brethren joined in an enthusiastic discussion of:
Masonic laws and customs, including custom~ within and without
the lodge, visitations, investigations committees, balloting, Masonic offenses. and Masonic related organizations;
Introduction to the symbolism of Masonry, the proper place of interpretation, a brief review of the three degrees and their relationship
one to another, and a beginning study into the depth of Freemasonry
which leads one to a new way of life.
We are pleased to report that the District voted to continue this
educational program and to make it an annual event. We express our
thanks to all concerned . particularly to Merle Doggett, Senior Warden
of Arcata Lodge No. 106 who served as chairman for this first meeting.
We acknowledge with a thank you this fine program and extend best
wishes for an even better program in future years.
A similar program was held in Los Angeles by West Gate Lodge
No. 335 and our Committeeman , Milton Ammann. had the pleasure of
attending and participating in this orientation course or education program designed especially for the Entered Apprentices, Fellowcrafts,
new M aster Masons and their wives. There were some 125 in attendance to share a program which included:
Introduction and remarks by the District Inspector, Brother Lloyd V.
Smith:
A review of the social activities and coaching program of the Lodge;
Masonry through the years. tenets and beliefs of Masonry. and
publications of the Grand Lodge;
Question and answer period.
We can think of no better way to launch an educational program or
to reactivate a lacking one than to follow one or both of the above formats and we pass them along in the hope that other lodges will follow
suit.
Incidentally Southern California Research Lodge reports that during
the first eight months of 1968, their speakers have responded to 57 requests to speak before Lodges. Masonic clubs or Masonic- related organi-

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
From the wisdom of Aristotle, we learn that:
"It is by education I learn to do by choice what other men may do
of fear."
constraint
by
It seems appropriate in the light of our long-standing program of
Masonic education that we occasionally pause to ask the questionWhat is Masonic Education?. The answe-r is set forth in your Lodge
M anual in the Masonic Education section and reads as follows:
.. In reality, this high-sounding phrase (Masonic Education) covers
a very simple idea. It is merely the gathering and sharing of knowledge
relative to the Institution of Freemasonry in its many aspects-its romantic history and beginnings, its high purpose and ideals: the meaning
of its ritualistic symbolism, its ethics and philosophy and the application
of all these aspects to everyday living and the improvement of man .
Around each of these subjects. a rich and interesting literature has developed over the past two hundred and fifty years and 'Masonic Education' is merely the process of acquaintancesh ip with others. This is
something that everyone can enjoy. no matter what his education or
background may be."
To my mind, the key word in our definition is "application." For
through Masonic education we gather and share information concerning
the history, symbolism and philosophy of our fraternity with one end
in view. Our sole purpose is to learn more so that we may the better be
enabled to apply the fundamental principles of Freemasonry to "everyday living and the improvement of man."
This is what we mean by Masonic Education.
During the past year, your Committee continued its assignment of
reviewing all Research Lodge materials intended for publication. The
officers of the Research Lodges have been cooperative and gracious in
acceptance of alteration or rejection when such was necessary. Emphasis
upon screening by qualified members of each Research Lodge has substantially improved and will ultimately benefit all concerned. The Committee commends the several Research Lodges on their publication
efforts and acknowledges this educational activity with appreciation and
recommends that every member in attendance at this Annual Communication visit the display area on the ground floor of the Temple and become familiar with the many fine papers available through the Research
Lodges. The nominal charge for these publications has been establ~shed
at or below actual cost of publication and handling . If you haven t already done so, please avail yourself of the opportunity to review these

\Vithout doubt, the finest educational endeavor of this past year was
made by our Grand Master who has most eloquently and most effectively
conveyed his theme of a "Rededication to the Fundamental Principles
of Freemasonry." He has drawn upon the trestleboard a most detailed
portfolio of how best the membership may apply our fraternity's principles to their daily lives. The results of his dedicated and inspired labors
will undoubtedly become more evident in the years to come. We join
the entire Grand Lodge in an expression of appreciation to Most Worshipful Eugene S. Hopp and assurance that we can do no less than
heed his words and his wisdom and put forth that extra effort as we
individually strive toward that perfect ashlar which exemplifies the true
Mason.

interest and support. This year's program begins at 7: 30 p.m. tonisrht

schedule and complete details (as amended) for both the classroom
sessions and for the general session on pages 18 and 19 of the Annual

program; we would, however, take just a few moments to call your especial attention to the second part of the program which will commence
at 8: 30 p.m. and which is open to all Master Masons. their families and
friends. Our Grand Master has graciously consented to host this general session and to present a special guest speaker and also a panel of
nationally recognized Masonic scholars who will speak on the Fundamental Principles of Freemasonry. I a m certain that you will agree that

enlightenment together with an added inducement in that we may share
this experience with our families and our friends. Join with us in this
unique evening of ''learn ( ing) to do by choice." A copy of the seminar
program is appended to this report as a matter of record.

Columbia : On May 5. 1968, two plots were sold in this cemetery
and Brother George Wishart Crichton was interred there. The other
grave was purchased by Mrs. Crichton for herself. Again this year our
committee man, Brother Marcel Baer, was successful in getting the
Future Farmers of America to spray both the Columbia and Jamestown Cemeterie s as a part of their project. This project by the group
from the Sonora High School adds to their treas ury and saves the Grand
Lodge a considerab le sum of money. The picket fence around the Columbia Cemetery was painted at a cost of $355.00. This is an expense that
will only incur about every five years. The cemetery is in a most presentable condition.
Jamestow n: Spraying for weeds and the usual cleanup is all that
has been necessary at the Jamestow n Cemetery . This area is surrounde d
by very large and beautiful oak trees. It will be necessary this year to
have some of these trimmed to preserve them and prevent future damage
to the cemetery. Several of the split rails in the fence have been broken
by falling limbs during storms and should be replaced. The necessary
funds for this work are included in our budget request.
Investigation is still continuing into the possibility and desirabilit y
of acquiring title to the Red Dog Cemetery , east of Grass Valley, and
the M ichigan City Cemetery . A complete report and recommen dation
will be made at the next Grand Lodge session. The possibility of forming these two cemeteries, along with several others, into a tax-suppo rted
district is also being investigat ed and in our opinion is to be desired.
Since the first part of this report was written several weeks ago several rather importAnt matters have come up.
No. I-Michig an Bluff.
The communit y of Michigan Bluff in Placer County has a cemetery
which is designated as the Masonic Cemetery. This cemetery dates
back to the beginning of the community. The plot is about one acre in
size. Like most of the other parcels in the communit y, it is on land that
has never been patented. The title rema ined with the Bureau of Land
Managem ent.
In 1963 the townspeop le began a survey and Trustee Township action with the Bureau of Land Managem ent through Judge Cameron of
Auburn. In September of this year the Trustee Townsite was awarded
to Judge Cameron.
At the time action on the Townsite was started, each of the parties
with a claim to land paid $50.00 into a fund for the preliminar y work.
Grand Lodge did not participat e in the study.
Final maps and metes and bounds descriptio ns are now being prepared for all parcels. When completed , they will be presented to Judge
Cameron. who will then issue grant deeds.

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON CEMETE RIES
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F . & A . M. of California:
Your Committe e on Cemeterie s respectful ly submits the following
report of their activities for the Masonic Year 1967-1968.
For the benefit of the Brethren who a re at tending Grand Lodge
for the first time, let us briefly give you a summary of the functions of
this committee . It is the duty of this committee to care for the three cemeteries which are owned by the Grand Lodge. To see that they are kept
in a condition that will reflect honor upon our fraternity. To work with
and counsel those individual lodges where cemetery care problems exist.
To see that sections set aside in public cemeteries for the exclusive use
of Masons do not deviate from our laws with respect to commercialism.
To study and inspect the plans for any monumen ts or altars to be erected
in such Masonic sections of public cemeteries, and make recommen dations to the Gra nd Master for his approval or disapprov al.
Fiddletow n Cemetery : Because of extensive work done at this cemetery throughou t the past few years very little care was required. Only
the spraying for weeds and a thorough cleanup. plus some minor repairs
that were necessary have been done. These are the only items of expense
that have been incurred. The budgted item for the installatio n of an
a dditional driveway gate has been expended at this time. The leaders
and other townspeop le of Fiddletow n have not reached full accord
among themselves and the property owners whose land adjoins our
cemetery. It is therefore suggested that the matter of the gate be held in
abeyance until some future developme nt points to the desirabilit y for
action.

the building of civilization. They were the visible and tangible evidence
of man's yearning for the infinite."
Many of us have demonstrated the allegiance to our country by
serving in its armed forces or by contributing in some other way. but
our responsibility of being exemplary in the discharge of our civil duties
does not stop there. A special duty rests upon you and me. as adults
and Masons, who still retain a belief in God and the moral order, to
influence the lives of others, particularly the alienated youth of this
tormented age. Those young people who, whether it be true or false.
feel that we, their elders, are at )e;ist in part to blame for their present
plight. If in no other way, we can do this by setting a good example for
them.
If you have visited our Home for Children at Covina, you probably
have seen posted on the bulletin board of the residence halls A Bill of
Rights and alongside it a corresponding Bill of Responsibilities. Although
each of the rights and responsibilities is worthy of remembrance and
emulation, I take time only to remind you of one right, "the right to
have a good example set by adults," and the corresponding responsibil~
ity, "to set a good example so that I may enjoy myself and influence
others."
What a splendid way to point up the double edged nature of good
citizenship. That going along hand in hand with each of our individual
rights as citizens is a corresponding responsibility to our fellow citizens.
Some of the trouble with our young people of today - and, yes, even
some of our adults - is that in their quest for freedom or liberty they
have forgotten. if they were ever told. that in our complex society there
must be some modifications and limitations upon personal freedom and
that their freedom stops where the other fellow's freedom begins.
George Washington, in a letter to Congress urging adoption of the
Constitution, wrote: "Individuals entering into society must give up a
share of liberty to preserve the rest. The magnitude of the sacrifice must
depend as well on the situation and the circumstances as on the object
to be obtained. "
In the concept of common law. freedom is a thing as native to man
as man . Coupled with freedom is a controlling moral sense that inspires
personal responsibility to fulfill man's obligations to himself. his fellow
men and to God. What disastrous results follow when the two are
divorced. The demand for freedom in the case of many of these young
men and women arises from a compulsion born. in turn, of a feeling of
personal responsibility to eliminate what they believe to be the evils of
contemporary society.
It has been said that America is fighting two wars, one in Vietnam,
the other at home. Perhaps we can afford to lose the one in Vietnam
but the one at home, that battle for the minds of our young people, must
be won at all costs. Somehow we will have to teach them that the place
to decide controversies. guilt or innocence. is in a court of law, not on

GRANO LODGE OP CA LIFORNIA

law mto their hearts and not their hands.

On a much earlier occasion, July 4, 1802, ninety-two years before
President McKinley's speech, Daniel Webster had this to say: "To
preserve the government we must also preserve a correct and energetic
tone of morals. After all that can be said, the truth is that liberty consists more in the habits of the people than in anything else. When the
public mind becomes vitiated and depraved, every attempt to preserve
it is vain. Laws are then a nullity, and constitutions waste paper. There
ace always men wicked enough to go to any length in the pursuit of
power if they can flnd others wicked enough to support them. They
regard not paper and parchment. Can you stop the progress of a usurper
by opposing to him the laws of his country? Then you may check the
careering winds or stay the lightning with a song. No. Ambitious men
must be restrained by the public morality. When they rise up to do evil.
they must flnd themselves standing alone. Morality rests on religion.
If you destroy the foundation, the superstructure must fall. In a world
of error, of temptation, of seduction; in a world where crimes often triumph. and virtue is scourged with scorpions-in such a world, certainly,
the hope of a hereafter is necessary to cheer and to animate. Leave us.
then, the consolations of religion. Leave to man. to frail and feeble man.
the comfort of knowing that when he gratifies his immortal soul with
deeds of justice, of kindness and of mercy. he is rescuing his happiness
from final dissolution and laying it up in heaven."
An age in the world's history has withered and died before our eyes
and a new age is strugHling to be born. the tone and direction of which
no man can tell and. whether we like it or not, we a re part of this new
age. To remain stationary is to lose ground. To repose is to fail. All of
us, therefore, whatever our age or station in life. must increase our
efforts so that we will not remain stationary. nor will we repose while
a world on the march passes us by. It is your duty. as it is mine, to
quicken our pace, to see that the eternally true values in our civilization .
those traditions that deserve to endure, are not swept away by the
torrent that now engulfs us all. No one of us ca n guarantee that his
efforts will be successful but eve1·y man can. at least. remove the cause
for rebuke that he did not try. And if. in trying. we expose certain
imperfections, what matter. for nothing would be done at all if a man
waited until he could do it so well that no one could flnd fault with it.
One of the most reliable standards by which our efforts may be
measured is the steadiness and persistence by which we cling to what
we believe to be right, the success we achieve in being true to ourselves.
for the familiar advice of Polonius has lost nothing of its forcefulness
for having so frequently been quoted-"To thine own self be true and
it must follow , as the night the day. thou canst not then be false to any
man."

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON TAXAT ION
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F . 5 A. M . of California:
Since filing our report for 1967, there have been changes in the payroll tax laws which apply to our various Masonic organizati ons.
As has been our custom in past years, we present. for reference purposes, the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various
payroll taxes which will be in effect during the calendar year 1969 and
thereafter .
FEDER.l\L WITHHOL DING (I NCOME) TAX

All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are subject to
Federal income tax withholdin g. In order to determine the amount of
income tax which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees , the
lodge should ask each employee to complete and file with the Secretary
o f the lodge a Federal Form W-4, "Employe e's Withhold ing Exemptio n
Certificate ." Reference to withholdin g tax tables furnished by the Treasury Departme nt will enable the Secretary to determine the amount to
to be withheld . New tables reflecting the 10% surtax should be in use
a t the present time.
FEDERAL IN SURANCE CONTRIBU TIONS (SOCIAL SECURITY )

As the law now stands, an employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject
to tax for each calendar quarter during which he earns $50.00 or more.
The ta x rates shown below are applicable to the first $7,800.00 of wages
paid to each employee during the calendar year. These rates are to be
paid by both the employer and the employee.

M asonic lodges will be subject to this tax if they employ four or
more individual s who are paid $50.00 or more per calendar quarter, providing they have first qualified as an "employe r" by employing four or
mo~e employees on at least one day in each of twenty or more weeks
durmg the calendar year. For this purpose, all paid employees of the
lodge. including the Secretary and those who are performin g ritualistic
services (Tiler, Organist, Soloist), should be counted if they receive
$50.00 or more per calendar quarter. Federal Unemploy ment Tax at the

to each employee during the calendar year. However, lodges which are

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF THE MASONIC CLUB
UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This is probably the final report we will render for the Masonic <:=tub
UCLA. A club that was organized in 1925 and through the enthusiasm
and contributions of Masons in Southern California, our clubhouse was
built and dedicated in 1929. This was at no cost to Grand Lodge. The
original cost. defrayed by contributions, was $140,219.00.
This club. for 39 years. was a recreational and social center for Masons, sons and daughters of Masons, Job's Daughters, Rainbow Girls,
and DeMolay boys in attendance at the University of California at Los
Angeles. It is from this same club that hundreds have graduated from
college. gone on into the world to make their places in society and, more
important. have become Masons and members of the Order of the
Eastern Star.
In a minority report by a member of this Board of Directors. given
at the las t Annual Communication, it was mentioned "within the past
year, we have read a nd heard publicity regarding the student strikes
and riots at both the Berkeley and UCLA campuses. I am proud to say
that not one incident of this lawlessness has occurred at either club." It
is particularly gratifying to report that although the clubhouse faciliti~s
are not available to the former members, they are, nevertheless, still
meeting as a Masonic affiliate club and carrying on their activities.
At the last Annual Communication, you voted to seU both clubhouses. At this writing. the Berkeley club has been sold for $270,000.
The special committee appointed by the Grand Master is now endeavor-

197

We know that the original contributions made by those Masons of
over 40 years ago was meant to build clubhouses at Berkeley and UCLA
for all those boys and girls of Masonic background and if they are not
given first preference, then we feel that we are breaking faith with those
early Masons. They established the corporations controlling the clubs
with the provision in their articles of incorporation that in the event of
the sale of the properties. the moneys so derived were to be turned over
to the Masonic Homes of California. This provision was modified just
this year in order that the moneys could be turned over to the California
Masonic Founda tion. It is our sincere hope and recommendation that
those boys and girls who were originally intended as recipients of the
club benefits be now preferentially considered.
The member~ of this Board will be eternally grateful for having had
the opportunity of serving the cause of clean and upright youth at the
Masonic Club UCLA and extend our thanks to the many Past Grand
Masters who have appointed us to serve on this Board. It is perhaps
trite to say now that the Masonic Clubhouses deserved a better fate.
The final and closing a udit report has been submitted to the Grand
Secretary's office. Obviously there is no request for an allocation of
funds to operate the club for the coming year.
Respectfully submitted,
BATES

w. MASON.

S. R o Y HowELL

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON OLD MASONIC HALL
IN LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on the Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles is pleased
to report the completion of all the work on the hall. located at 416Yi
North Main Street, Los Angeles.
A balcony, beautifully produced by artisans in wood and steel. has
been erected and an attractive rail has been installed.
Work is progressing rapidly on the other buildings in the complex.
particularly the Merced Theater and the Old Pico House, which are
adjacent to the Old Lodge Hall.
The rooms below the hall have been leased to the Security-Pacific
National Bank. They plan to decorate the interiors in the charming
decor of the style in vogue during the early days of Los Angeles. The
bank has called experts to see their quarters complement the rest of the
complex.
The budget allocated to the hall in the past will be sufficient until
the final completion of the entire State Park complex. At that time, it
will be necessary for us to have a full time guide, since all of the buildings will be open to the public five or six days a week.
Brother Wray Gibson is doing a fine job of showing the visitors
through the Old Temple and keeping its displays shining and immaculate.
The hall is open only on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. from 12
noon until 5 p.m. I urge all Masons and sojourners in the area to visit
this historic shrine which has been faithfully restored to match the .first
meeting hall of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42. now in its I 16th year of
devotion and service to the Craft.
Many lodges in and around the Los Angeles area have used the
Old Temple as a meeting place to confer degrees, but the activity should
be publicized. Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814 meets regularly
there on Thursday nights. However, the Hall is available on the other
week nights for degree work to any Lodge in California.

liRAND LODGE OP C ALIFORNIA

199

There is ample parking across the street from the Old Hall. The
streets are well lighted and patrolled. There are also many fine restaurants in the area for dining. before or after "work" in the Temple.
Your committee is deeply appreciative of the splendid support, concern and cooperation in restoring and maintaining the Old Temple.
whose hallowed halls will ever ring with the muted voices of a golden
past.
Respectfully submitted,
BENJAMIN M. WEISS, Chairman
HERBERT HARGRAVE. JR.
LLOYD E. PARKER

by

of

share-t his made the stock we received worth $742.500.00 The facts
were related to the Investm ent Commit tee, and at its meeting on June
12, 1968, the Commi ttee authoriz ed the sale of the shares at the market,
on t.h e recomm endatio n of Moody 's Investo rs Service. our Investm ent
Counse l. The shares are listed on the New York Stock Exchap ge. For

Cl?AN O LODGE O F CAUPOR NIA

profession al talent will have to be employed for the purpose, in order
that we may be assured of a technically satisfacto ry completion of the
project.
We therefore recommend, assuming the continuati on of a special
committee on code revision, that a new program of procedure be developed which will have the concurren ce of the special committee and of
the elected Grand Lodge line officers. It should be recognized that a
procedure , once adopted, must then be followed through to its conclusion
and that this may require several years of study and work.
We do not wish to leave the impression that nothing has been accomplished during the three years of the life of this special committee.
A substantia l amount of work, under the leadership of Past Grand
Master Ellsworth Meyer, who chaired the committee during its first two
years, has formed the basis of approach to the task. This very work,
however, has made it completel y apparent that the revision of the California Masonic Code must be done carefully, painstakin gly. thoughtfully, and with the united concurren ce of a great many individuals.
Respectfu lly submitted,
THEODOR E MERIAM, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETIREMENT PLAN
To the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M . of California:
The Masonic Homes of Califorina Retirement Plan. effective Jan uary 1. 1955. became fully implemented by instrument dated December 8.
1958. at which time the various employees of the Boards of •Relief. etc ..
were put under the Plan and it w as put into effect. Grand Lodge employees were placed under the Plan effective Janua ry 1, 1956.
The original Plan was administered by a pension committee composed of the entire Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California .
The amended Plan covering all employees of Grand Lodge. Masonic
Homes and affiliated groups is now governed by a committee, three of
whom are selected by the Homes Board and two by the Grand Master.
This committee. as stated by its then Chairman. the late Brother
Arthur M. Warren, P.G.M .. in the 1961 Report, "is charged with the
full responsibility of administering the Plan in accordance with its written terms.
Among its responsibilities are the following:
1. Approval of requests for early retirement.
2. Approval of requests for disability retirement.
3. Approval of optional retirement requests.
4. Approval of requests for continuance of employment after retirement date has been reached, and establishment of condition
of such employment."
There are other determinations which become the responsibility of
the Retirement Plan Committee, such as determining the amount of
money essential to keep the Plan fully funded . Employees under the
Plan contribute 3% of their annual salaries. The employer contributes
the balance required as determined by the actuary. These fu nds are
deposited with the Trustee. Wells Fargo Bank.
During the period under review your Committee, in accordance w ith
the duties as outlined. did pass all applications for retirement.
As of January 1. 1968. 116 Masonic Homes employees and 25 employees of Grand Lodge and component organizations participated in
the Plan. The Masonic Homes maintained eighteen employees on retirement. Grand Lodge and components had twelve retired employees.
Respectfully submitted .
ALFRED F. BRESLAU ER. Chairman
PHIL N. MYERS
LAURENCE E. DAYTON

PAUL A. PFLUEGER
PAUL F. BALCK

Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
There has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes that portion of the report of the Board of Trustees of the
· California Masonic Memorial Temple relating to the raising of funds
by a per capita tax, and the establishing of a reserve for the specific
purpose of developing library and museum facilities.
Your Committee in 1967 expressed itself in accord with the objective
as stated in the first paragraph of the resolution. We again are in accord
and believe that it is now time to move forward with the purchase of
real property for the purpose.
The amount of the per capita tax is properly the concern of the
Committee on Finance and we have no recommendation on this matter.
Except for that portion we recommend the adoption of the resolution.

I therefore move the adoption of the resolution and report that the
Committee recommends a "yes"vote.
A majority voted against the resolution .
