GRAND LODGE EXPENDIT URES

Review
This subject is limited to reimburse ment for Grand Lodge Officers ,
Inspectors . Committe emen and members of Boards for expenses in performing their respective duties, and to Past Grand Officers, Masters and
Wardens or duly elected representa tives in attending the Annual Communication. It does not extend into the realm of salaries and general
administra tive costs of the Grand Secretary 's Office, the Memorial Temple, or the Masonic Homes.
The Committe e on Finance prepares a budget which is presented to
Grand Lodge and. when adopted, this constitute s an appropriat ion of
money. CMC 193. The same Committe e presents a recommen ded per
capita contributi on to cover the budgeted expenses .
The preparatio n of the budget by the Finance Committe e is done
following consultati on with Grand Lodge officers and committee chairmen. It is finalized after action on committee reports and the Grand
Master's recommen dation at the Annual Communi cation.
The topic does not end there. however, for as the year progresses
the Grand Master's program may require more than has been allocated,
or a committee may justifiably exceed its allowance in effecting the
Grand Lodge program, and the CMC provides no express relief. In
practice, supplemen tary appropriat ion requests made by the Grand
Master are honored and such actions are approved at the following
Grand Lodge Communi cation. We hereinafte r submit a recommen dation
for legislation affirming the propriety of this practice.
Furthermo re, budgeting of funds for designated purposes does not
mean that they can or should be always spent. All invoices and expense
accounts of members entitled to reimburse ment are reviewed prior to
payment but the CMC is not uniform on the method of review. Some
accounts are required to be approved by the Grand Master, Masonic
Homes Endowme nt Board ( CMC 248). and Board of Control ( CMC
266). Others are reviewed by the Grand Secretary 's office as part of the
administra tive functions of his office. However, we find no express authority in the CMC for this pra<:tice.
After expense claims are submitted for payment by members entitled
ent. the office reviews them individual ly and payments

the figure of $10.800.00 has been carried in the budget. Present and
future programs contempla ted indicate that this amount is inadequat e
and should be increased. The Grand Master need render only a general
account of expenses incurred by him.

Grand Warden. the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary 's expenses

Hawaii
There are ten Lodges in Hawaii with a total membership of approximately 3000. and many of these Brethren reside outside of Hawaii.
It has been _customary for Grand Lodge to make reimbursement for
some expenses mcurred for instruction in the ritual and for air travel of
three ~nspectors, ten Lodge officers, and one Grand Lodge officer in
attendmg the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
A1! analysis has been made of revenue from our Brethren in Hawaii
~nd d1sbur~emen~s made in their behalf, including but not limited to the
items mentlo~ed m the foregoing paragraph. It is found that from a fac;
tu~l standpoint the revenue is insufficient to credit the Hawaiian Lodges
with_ equal contribution, on a pro rata basis, as is derived frorn the Californta Lodges, for the operating expenses of Grand Lodge and of the
Masonic Homes. In other words, California Lodges make up any deficit
needed for the benefit of Hawaiian Lodges.
Irrespective of this observation, it is believed that the Grand Lodge.
.
m continuing its Masonic affiliation with the Brethren in Hawaii, for the
general good of the Order, should go even further.
Your committee therefore recommends:
( 1 ) That allowance to Hawaiian Brethren for expenses incurred for
.
~nstruction in the ritual, and "pay of members" for Lodge officers attending the Annual Communication, be continued ;
( 2) That the Hawaiian Inspectors be reimbursed on the same formula as California Inspectors when attending the Annual Communication ;
( 3) That the incumbent Grand Lodge Officer from Hawaii be re-

(NOTE: Guy B. Mize, a member of the Committee. did not sign
the above report but presented the following minority report in the form
of a letter of dissent to its Chairman.}
HERBERT A. HUEBNER

Junior Grand Warden
610 South Broadway
Los Angeles. Cal. 90014

August 17, 1968

Dear Herb:
It has been a pleasure to serve with you and the other members of
the Special Finance Study Committee which has been working on the
problems assigned to it at the last Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge--problems which have been of considerable concern to me in
my capacity as a member of the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance.
I am sorry that I could not accommodate you and the other members
of the committee by joining in the signing of the report. thus making
support of the report unanimous as it is presented to Grand Lodge. I
believe, however, that it was c:lear to all members of the committee. from

225

When I was asked to become a member of the Finance Committee
and to serve as its chairman, I was well aware of the provisions in the
Masonic Code relating to the powers of the Finance Committee. I was
also aware , through long years of friendship with my predecessor who
served as chairman of the Finance Committee. of his concern and desire
for the committee to be fully effective, to the greatest degree, in the interest of Grand Lodge-and our Brethren.
In assuming and pursuing my duties I made it clear that the Finance
Committee would not encroach into other areas of Masonic service-nor has it knowingly done so. Yet it has been inferred that Finance has
tried to establish policy when criticism has been offered on expenditures
not contemplated in the Budget-particularly when expenditures were
for departures from past and sensible practices and for innovations
which the Brethren might not approve.
I was encouraged in my first year of chairmanship of Finance when
Grand Master Smith was sympathetic to the idea-and desirabilityof broadening the Masonic Code to firm ly establish the powers of
Finance to represent Grand Lodge in the same fashion as would a comparable committee for a well-run business establishment. Not just a
committee which v.;ould meet, put figures in the form of requests for
appropriations together-and then present them to Grand Lodge under
the label of a Budget.
The latter, in my opinion, is what the Special Finance Study Committee Report will accomplish, if adopted by Grand Lodge.
During the Grand Lodge year ended October 13. 1967, and by
direction of Grand Lodge based upon a recommendation by Gra nd
Master Smith , a year long analysis of Grand Lodge operations relating
to finance was made by the Finance Committee, it being deemed to be
the proper committee to make such an analysis.
A fairly comprehensive report was prepared and presented to Grand
Master Dayton for his review. It was recognized that the report. with
all its recommendations, was not in complete enough form to be presented to Grand Lodge and it was agreed that the report be referred to a
new committee for additional work and study-the committee which
you have chaired this year.
The present Special Study Report, controversial as it may be in
some of its conclusions and recommendations, will. if approved, make

227

GRAND LODGE O P CALIPORNIA

equitable, to a considerable degree, the treatment of expenses of those
engaged in serving Masonry at the Grand Lodge level. Recognition of
gross inequities was observed by the Finance Committee and steps to
correct them were included in the prior report by the Finance Committee.

as provided for in the Report. This includes affairs to which Grand
Lodge Officers are asked to bring their wives at Grand Lodge expense.
I am concerned as to where this will lead us in years to come-as other
la~orers in the ~i~eyards seek equal benefits for their s ervices. I spell
this out because 1t 1s spelled out in the Report as new policy.

226

My dissent is based in part on the fact that there appears to be. in
the minds of some present Grand Officers and members of this Special
Study Committee, a feeling that there is a "conflict of interest" when the
Grand Secretary. or members of his staff, and/ or the Finance Committee exercise interest. in whatever manner, in the expenditure of Grand
Lodge funds-whethe r provided for in the Budget or to be covered by
supplemental appropriations .
I consider the office of the Grand Secretary and, certainly. including
its present incumbent, to be best suited and best qualified to evaluate
expense claims fairly and impartially. and I have to object to removal of
authority or control in this phase from the Grand Secretary's office.
Certainly, if the objection stems from the possible use of any signiflcant
portion of his time in the purely mechanical features of expense control,
necessary additional help could be provided the Grand Secretary just
as easily as the Report makes provision for employment of help. if needed. by the proposed new Audit Committee.
On the subject of the Audit Committee, it seems to me. reading the
sections of the Report which treat of the Audit Committee, that its
powers and functions are so circumscribed and limited, it will be just
another committee gracing the Grand Lodge roster. The real responsibilities which have been undertaken by the Grand Secretary and
the Finance Committee are not given to the Audit Committee.
All real control of expenditures will be restricted to a few Grand
Officers, committee and board chairmen, who may not at all times have
a complete grasp of the financial structure and problems of Grand Lodge.
It can be easily argued that "conflict of interest," if such a thing really
exists. might enter more easily under this proposal than under our present procedures.
As suggested earlier in this letter of dissent, I am concerned that, in
actuality, the committee preparing the annual budget is to be restricted
solely to that function and, consequently, will hardly merit the title of
Finance Committee-a misnomer under the circumstances.
In considering the Special Finance Study Committee Report, members of Grand Lodge should weigh carefully what is proposed in the
way of controls-as opposed to practices engaged in now a nd in the
past.
Although in favor of liberalized and equitable policies relating to expense claims, I still oppose the permissive and broadened base for
expense claims for ce.r tain types of nonofficial Grand Lodge aft'airs-

. In short, recognizing the powers of the Grand Master, and not seeking und.uly to abridge them, I feel that, if the Special Finance Study
Report is ~dopted as now written, shearing the Grand Secretary's office
and ~he Finance Committee .of duties which they are capable of per~ormmg, have been performmg, and are willing to perform, the best
mterests of the Fraternity are not being served.
Sincerely and fraternally,
Guv B. M1zE. P.G.M..

Th e C ommittee on Finance:
The Report of Special Finance Study Committee has been referred
to your Committee on Finance.
The Report recommends increased expense allowances for Grand
Lodge Officers, commit~eemen, board members and representatives , in
order to more fully reimburse them for their necessary expenses in
performing their respective duties.
There is a further recommendation as to specific allowance schedules
to more properly deflne necessary expenditures in order to liberalize
payments and at the·same time to eliminate abuses.
. The Report further recommends the establishment of an Audit Committee for the purpose of approving submitted claims for payment within
established categories.
Your Committee on Finance has conflned its consideration to the
fina.ncial effect on the budget of Grand Lodge and the resulting per
capita assessment.
Your Committee is unable to present a reliable forecast of the increase~ .cost and resulting impact upon the per capita assessment. W e
have diligently examined our present costs and, by consultation with the
Deputy Grand Master and several members of the Special Committee
'
have secured their best estimates of the possible cost increase.
The.re is ~ood reason to believe that under this recommended program there will be a substa ntial increase in the number of Grand Lodge
~embers claiming reimbursement although some will undoubtedly contmue. as at present. to absorb a portion, or all. of their expenses .
Afte: ~e necessary rules and regulations, including the schedules
of per~1ss1bl~ allowances, have been established, the task of proper
budgeting will be greatly simplified. At the moment. however, your

Committee can only estimate, to the best of its ability, the increase in per
capita cost as a result of the adoption of this report. .
· Our best estimate of the increased cost of this program comes to
$82,000.00 minimum or an approximate 35 cent increase in the per capita
assessment.
In the course of our review of the Report we noted that, as the report
now stands, there may be some possibility of overlapping payments to
claimants. If the Grand Master·s Recommendation No. 3 be adopted,
we therefore suggest that the specific allowance schedules be drawn
most carefully.

The Committe.e on Policy and General Purposes:
The report of the Special Finance Study Committee and Recommendation No. 3 of the Grand Master have been referred to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Grand Master recommends that the report of this special committee "be adopted in principle and that the Special Finance Study
Committee be requested to prepare the necessary rules and regulations
to implement the recommendations of the report and that these (the
rules and regulations) shall be effective on approval by the Grand
Master."
It appears to your committee that by an adoption in principle_ must
mean an adoption of any and all policies which can be fo~nd m the
report and as to matters contained in the report but as to wh1~h ~atters
of policy are not stated or only partially stated, the determmatton of
the policy of the Grand Lodge is to be delegated to several officers on
the one hand and on the other hand to persons not designated by the
report.
It is readily apparent that as to many matters. the report contemplates substantial changes from policies and procedures which have been
established for a number of years. As to other matters, a reading of the
report indicates that perhaps changes of policy will be formulated ~nd
put into effect between the close of this Communication and the openmg
of the next Annual Communication.
The report embraces the expenditures of all constituent l~ges, both
permissible expenditures and prohibited expenditures. Sue~ is a large
field and involves substantial sums. It also embraces the reimbursement
of expenses of the 28 officers of the Grand Lodge, the more than 100 Inspectors and more than 300 members of the numerous committ~es of
the Grand Lodge. Again the number of persons and the funds directly
involved are substantial.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes does not believe
that·the policy of the Grand Lodge as to such matters should be left to a
numerically small segment of the Grand Lodge. We believe the Grand

GR!\N D LODGE OF CALIFO RNIA

229

Lodge and only the Grand Lodge should determine what its policy
shall be.
To discuss all the matters within the embrace of the report would
unduly encroach upon the time available, but we shall point to a few
specifics, particularly instances in which the report states or infers that
changes should be made or are likely to be made by rules and regulations
to be formulated between this date and the opening of the next Annual
Communication.
The special committee has divided its report into two parts. The
first part is relative to expenditures by lodges and consists of pages 3,
4 and 5 of the report. A portion of page 3 lists the sources of revenue
of lodges, two-thirds of page 3 and one- half of page 4 are devoted to
a list of expenditures by lodges which are either permitted or prohibited.
the particular section of our code or annotation therein permitting or
prohibiting a given expendtiure is stated. This tabulation should be a
handy reference to Masters, Wardens and Secretaries.
The tabulation is followed by five recommendations by the special
study committee.
Recommendation No. 1 states that a recent amendment to Section
409 of the California Masonic Code "may be interpreted to authorize
some use of lodge funds or property to subsidize youth organizations. It
would be preferable," the report reads, " that any ambiguity be removed
by clarifying legislation with some definition of limitations and we so
recommend." The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is at a
loss to know whether the request that this recommendation "be adopted
in principle" is a request the Grand Lodge interpret the amendment to
mean (I ) that lodge funds may be used to subsidize youth organizations
or ( 2) that they may not be used, or ( 3) merely that an ambiguity exists.
If it is a request for a Grand Lodge declaration that funds may be so
used, it would be better policy to defer the declaration until the clarifying
legisla tion was before the Grand Lodge and no valid purpose would be
served by an approval in principle. If the request is for a declaration that
funds may be so used, it would be better to wait until the extent of the
use, one percent, five, ten or twenty percent of annual revenue or some
other measure of use has been su9gested. before the matter is approved
in principle. If the request is merely for a determination that an ambiguity exists and clarifying legislation is desirable, no valid purpose
would be served by an adoption in principle.
Recommendation 2 states : "Constituent lodges should not contribute
to the Inspector's expenses in attending the Annual Communication."
Recommendation 3 states that there is a custom at an Annual Communication for "one or a group of Inspectors to host a breakfast or luncheon
where present or past Grand Officers are invited together with voting
officers or •.. elected representatives as guests of the Inspectoral Dis-

230

231

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRANO LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

. We approve," states the report, "the use of Lodge refreshtrict.
ment funds for this purpose when desired but recommend that the expenditure be limited to include the above specified guests." At least two
questions are raised by Recommendations 3 and 4-first, if the policy
is approved that lodges should not subsidize Inspectors in attending
an Annual Communication wherein lies the desired consistency of a
policy to subsidize him as the host of a breakfast or luncheon during
that communication? The second question is: If the Grand Lodge should
approve "in principle" the use of lodge funds to pick up the tab for past
and present Grand Lodge officers and voting members of its own and
of any other lodge. why should the Grand Lodge decree that the lodge
cannot pick up the tab for its own secretary unless he is a Past Master
or for a distinguished guest from another jurisdiction? No such limitations would apply if the breakfast or luncheon we.re held in its own
temple. Why should such a policy of discrimination be started? The
Committee on Policy and General Purposes does not recommend that
you so discriminate.
The second part of the report is concerned with reimbursement of
Grand Lodge officers and committeemen. It is proposed therein to create
a new committee, to be known as the Audit Committee and create
categories, as the report calls them, seven in number.

by the Audit Committee. The report provides for chairmen to pass upon
their own expense claims.
If the Audit Committee questions any certified claim, it may present
the claim to the Grand Master for determination.
While it might be argued that the officers and chairmen who would
be authorized to certify that expenses were incurred in the discharge of
the duties of the claimant were the persons who best knew whether the
expenses were so incurred. we do not believe that it is good policy to
have a host, and they are a host, of officers and chairmen passing upon
whether staying at the Ritz Hotel or the Hotel Modest was a proper or
necessary expense.
It appears that adoption of the report in principle at this time would
inaugurate a policy to which it would be unrealistic to expect any measure of uniformity. One chairman might feel that it was necessary that he
and the members of his committee should stay and dine at Hotel De
Luxe, while another might decide that Hotel B was sufficient.
Our committee notes that as to the categories in which the Grand
Chaplain, Grand Orator, Grand Marshal and Grand Tiler are placed:
that in which certain other appointive officers are placed, the category
of Inspectors, the category of chairmen, members and consultants of
committees are placed, this report contemplates appropriations for
and allowances of necessary expenses and that the term necessary
expenses is at least in part defined; however, in the categories of the
Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens. Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, Grand Lec~urer and Assistant Grand Lecturers the report provides that the budget shall provide for their expenses. The qualifying
adjective "necessary" does not appear.
Your committee does not recommend the adoption of a policy or
the report which thus creates a double standard. We prefer a system
such as that now used in the matter of miles traveled-namely, a flat
rate. If reimbursement for hotels, meals and other items were set at a
specified sum each, innumerable headaches would be avoided, auditing
would be vastly simplified and all Brethren should be happy.
To get the report of the Special Finance Study Committee and Recommendation No. 3 before the house. I move that said report be approved in principle.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes unanimously recommends a "no" vote,

1967 GRAND MAsTER's RECOMMEND ATION No. 5

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In his message to the 1967 communicat ion, the Gra~~ Master sp?ke
concerning our law which prevents a Lodge from r~ce1vmg an applic.ation for the degrees from a man who has been convicted of the commission of a crime. He recommende d that the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes and the Committee on Jurispruden ce restudy the
entire subject and report to this communicat ion. He su99ested that the
two committees propose any legislation necessary .to mo:e clearly define
the policy of the Grand Lodge or to implement its policy. The Grand
Lodge approved the recommenda tion.
Each committee independent ly pursued its study. The two chai~men
communicat ed to each other the results and found the two committees
were in complete accord.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has examined the
existing statutory law, decisions by Grand Masters, both approved and
disapproved , and committee reports. It has conc.lud~d that the Grand
Lodge has established a policy and that the policy is the correct one.
The committee believes that the policy of the Grand Lodge should be
spelled more clearly as to the effect of a pardon under t"."'o differe~t sets
of circumstanc es. The Committee on Jurispruden ce adv1.se~ that 1t does
not deem any further action is necessary to effect the ex1stmg policy but
that action is necessary as to the effect of a pardon under the different
circumstance s.
The only statutory provision is that portion of Section 511 of the
California Masonic Code which reads: "An applicant for the degrees
of Masonry must be ... of moral conduct .. . "The section was adopted
in 1947 but for all intents and purposes was merely a restatement or
rearrangeme nt of statutory language which had existed for many years.
In 1957 four resolutions were introduced by two members. Some
were presented as alternatives if others were not adopted. They were
withdrawn by the two proponents when the Committ~e on Juris~rudence
presented its own version of a short but comprehens ive resolutio~; Th.e
resolution proposed by the Committee was adopted. It reads: ~e it
further resolved that a person who has pleaded guilty or been convicted
in the courts of a crime which is morally wrong in itself is not eligible
to apply for the degrees." The committee did not propose tha_t the language be made a part of the California Masonic Code, hence.it appears
only in the annotations under Section 511 of our code and is lettered.
Let no mistake be made; although the small paragraphs which the Code
Commission has placed under many sections of the code are. not themselves sections or subsections of the code. but are merely printed there

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

233

to inform the reader how the section above has been interpreted from
time to time in the past, nevertheless the annotations disclose the policy
which the Grand Lodge has established.

It should be noted that neither Section 511 nor the resolution adopted
in 1957 uses the term felony or any words about the serving of a term
in prison or any other institution. The present policy of the Grand Lodge
is concerned with "moral conduct" and whether the "crime . . . was
morally wrong in itself." Neither the section nor the resolution is concerned with whether the crime is classified as a felony or a misdemeano r
under the law of the State of California or the jurisdiction in which it
it was committed.
In general terms, whether a guilty plea or a conviction amounts to
a felony or only a misdemeano r depends on the action taken or sentence
imposed by the trial court. On the other hand, the policy of this Grand
Lodge is to make eligibility or ineligibility depend upon the nature of
the act committed.
The fact that the availability of the automatic expulsion provisions
in our code are dependent upon whether the conviction of one of our
members was of a felony or a misdemeano r should not be confused
with our policy as to eligibility or ineligibility to apply for the degrees.
The two policies of the Grand Lodge in these two different fields are
also different.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that persons who have pleaded guilty, nolo contendere or have been convicted
of a crime which is· morally wrong in itself should be ineligible to apply
for our degrees. We therefore have no motion to make in that regard.
Prior to the adoption in 1957 of the resolution to which we have
called attention, Grand Master Arthur Warren announced a decision
that a man who had been convicted of a felony but had received a commuted sentence by a presidential pardon, had not served any time in a
prison and appeared to have become rehabilitated was nevertheless
ineligible to apply for our degrees. The Committee on Jurispruden ce
recommende d tha t Grand Lodge approve the decision and it did. The
circumstanc es under which the commutatio n was issued do not appear.
It might be inferred that regardless of the circumstanc es under which a
pardon was issued, the applicant was ineligible. We are of the opinion
that our policy should be that in those very few instances in which a
pardon was signed because it was subsequentl y established that a convicted man had not committed the crime that such a man should be
eligible to apply and that in the more numerous instances in which a
pardon is issued as an act of grace, that is as an act of executive clemenc·y only, he should not be eligible because he did, indeed, commit an
act which was morally wrong in itself and he has not been "of good
moral conduct."

The Committee on Jurisprudence will present proposed legislation
to implement this policy and our committee ·recommends a "yes" vote
thereon.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Past Grand Master Laurence E. Dayton recommended to the 1967
Communication of Grand Lodge that the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes and the Committee on Jurisprudence reconsider and
report on the ineligibility of applicants for membership who have criminal records (Recommendation No. 5). It was requested that the report
of these committees be ready for the 1968 Grand Lodge Communication.
These two committees have now considered the subject assigned to
them and have recommended, as a matter of polky, that no person who
has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to or been convicted of a felony,
or a misdemeanor which is morally wrong. shall be eligible for the degrees of Masonry unless for the reason that he did not commit the
crime, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of conviction
vacated .
It should be noted that with the exception of the provision relating
to pardon or the vacation of a judgment of conviction . this general policy
determination was enacted into Masonic law by a 5/ 6 vote of Grand
Lodge in 1957 and is now contained in Section 51 lo of the Masonic
Code.
Pursuant to the above, the Committee on Jurisprudence proposes a
new section of the Masonic Code, to be numbered Section 513 (thus
taking the number of a section repealed in 1966) .
The following resolution is presented:
"RESOLVED: That a new Section 513 be added to the Callf~rnia
Masonic Code in form as follows:
'Section 513: A person who has pleaded guilty or nolo
contendere or has been convicted in the courts of a felony.
or a misdemeanor which is morally wrong in itself, is not
eligible to apply for the degrees of Masonry unless for the
reason that he did not commit the offense, he either has
been pardoned, or had his judgment of convicUon vacated.'
and that annotations 511 g, h, I. o, p and q be deleted from the California
Masonic Code."
The Committee moves the adoption of the resolution and recommends a "yes"vote.

The Committee on Finance:
There has been referred to the Committtee on Finance Resolution
No. 1, which provides for changes in voting procedures in Grand Lodge
and suggests the use of voting machines.
The Committee on Finance reviewed the practicality and cost of
utilizing voting machines with the office of Registrar of Voters of the
City and County of San Francisco. Such machines are available on a
rental basis whereby the rental cost is $20.00 for the first day and $5.00
per day thereafter. The machines weigh approximately 800 pounds and
occupy a space of approximately 5 feet by 3Yi feet. Cartage charges
to and from the warehouse are estimated at $75.00 per machine. It is
estimated that we would require approximately twelve machines for
our purpose. At least two technicians at approximately $10.00 per man

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

239

hour will also be required for programming and for general supervision
of the equipment during voting. It is doubtful that the trained technicians are members of the Craft and their entry into the Temple during
our working sessions would be awkward, if not impractical. Further,
we are informed that it would not be practical to attempt to train members of Grand Lodge to serve in this capacity.
Summing up the costs cited above, we estimate a total cost of
$1300.00 for the first day's operation.
While we appreciate the spirit in which the resolution was offered.
we feel the additional expense is not warranted and recommend a "no"
vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution number one, if adopted, would eliminate the present authorization in section thirty-nine of the California Masonic Code that
a vote may be by voice or by rising. The resolution would require that
all action on proposed amendments to the code "and on all other matters
requiring voting except the election of officers" be taken on one ballot,
preferably through the use of voting machines.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that the
proposed resolution would require the impossible. For example, there
were thirty-three resolutions filed with the Grand Secretary for consideration at this communication; last year fifty-eight were presented. It
is true that these could be printed on a single ballot in advance of the
start of a communication but the voting members would be required to
keep in mind the arguments for and against each resolution until all
had been discussed and then cast one ballot on all of them. Such a procedure would cast an intolerable burden on those in attendance.
In many instances resolutions in the same general field may overlap
in some particulars and be inconsistent in other particulars, if the vote
is taken at one time on all resolutions conflicts in law may be created.
A question arises as to which resolution would control inasmuch as
each was adopted at the same moment. How many hours would it take
to tabulate 1500 or more ballots as to forty or fifty items?
There are more votes taken during any communication on matters
contained in reports of committees than the number of votes taken on
resolutions filed with the Grand Secretary: if this resolution were a dopted these w ould have to be included on the single ballot. How this could
physically be accomplished is not apparent.
The use of voting machines under this resolution would be optional
but preferred. One of our committee members recently attended a convention at which voting machines were used. Separate votes were taken
on the machines on a number of propositions, not a single vote on thirty,
forty or fifty matters as this resolution would require. The number of

241

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP C.\LIFORNIA

voting delegates was approximately one-half of the number of votes
cast here. There were eight machines being used and a crew of skilled
mechanics to operate them. He advises that the shortest period in which
a single vote was taken was eighteen minutes and the longest an hour
and a half.
We hesitate to guess how many machines would be required here
or how many hours would be required for 1500 or more men to throw
thirty. forty or fifty levers each.
In order to get the resolution before the house, I move the adoption
of resolution number one.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a no
vote.

WHEREAS, majority rule is basic in all American governmental
units both in the election of officers of these units and in the conduct of
legislative business of these units, and
WHEREAS, the conduct of Masonic business at Grand Lodge relative to changing provisions of the California Masonic Code is restricted
by rules which subject that body to minority rule in that 5/ 6 of the members voting must consent to a change before it can be made, which means
that 1 / 6 of the members voting (plus one) can prevent all proposed
changes in the C.M.C..
BE IT RESOLVED that all voting in the Grand Lodge shall be
based on majority rule, so that any proposed change in the C.M .C . shall
carry and be effective if it receives an affirmative vote of one more than
half of the members voting.
Respectfully submitted.

The Committee on Jurisprudence.:
This resolution proposes that all voting in Grand Lodge. except for
the election of officers, shall be on one ballot "preferably through use
of voting machines."
. The resolution does not point out, however, what amendments are
to be made to the law, nor how the proposal shall be accomplished, nor
how or when a single ballot could be made up, nor how voting machines
could be used, nor even suggest an appropriation for their purchase.
The proposal is simply impossible of accomplishment and legislation cannot be drawn to effect it. Such a procedure is not applicable to
a parliamentary body such as the Grand Lodge. At each Annual Communication at least fifty to sixty separate votes are taken , such as upon
recommendations of the Grand Master, resolutions presented by members prior to the required ninety day period, and on recommendations
and resolutions presented by committees such as Charters, Finance and
Grievances. Many of these votes occur during and up to the very end
of the business session, after discussion or debate on each, and after
reports of the various committees. Many of these recommendations and
r·e solutions cannot be anticipated. They .' cannot possibly be voted on a
single ballot.
Accordingly, the Committee on Jurisprudence has drawn no legislation and recommends a no vote on the rsolution.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution 1A proposes the adoption of a rule that if a proposed
amendment to the California Masonic Code "receives an affirmative vote
of one more than half of the members voting" the proposed amendment
shall be effective. The resolution does not present the two amendments
which would be necessary to accomplish the purpose of the proponents.
At the present'time it is provided in both divisions of our code that
in order for an amendment to be adopted at the first communication at
which it is proposed it must receive a five-sixths affirmative vote. It is
further provided that if it does not receive a five-sixths vote but does
receive a majority vote, it shall be carried over to the next annual communication, at which time it shall be declared adopted if it receives a
two-thirds affirmative vote.
The thinking of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes is
reflected in the fact that twice in recent years it has recommended the
adoption of proposed amendments to reduce the required vote from
five-sixths to two-thirds; however, the committee does not believe that
the policy of the Grand Lodge should be that the five-sixths should be
reduced to a mere majority.
In order to get the resolution before the house, I move its adoption
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that
you vote "no" on it.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 2 proposes to eliminate the rights of certain Grand
and Past Grand Officers in voting.
A careful analysis of the effect of this resolution if adopted discloses
that it would eliminate a total of 26 votes now enjoyed by Grand Lodge
Officers, including that of the Grand T ·r easurer, Grand Secretary and
Grand Lecturer and up to, at present, a possible 17 votes by the Past
Grand Officers.
We a.re of the opinion that this small percentage of the total vote
cannot directly or indirectly amount to "control of the Grand Lodge"
and the fact that these Brethren, having served the Grand Lodge far
beyond the call of duty, are entitled to this small token of our honor
and esteem.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This resolution proposes that only the Grand Master, the Deputy
Grand Master, the Senior Grand Warden and the Junior Grand Warden be entitled to vote as Grand Lodge Officers; that the Past Grand
Masters collectively have one vote.
Its effect would be to prevent twenty-three of the twenty-seven
Grand Lodge officers from voting in that capacity, and would cause
those present of the nineteen living Past Grand Masters to cast a single
collective ballot.
To give effect to the concept of the proposed resolution, it appears
to the Committee on Jurisprudence to be necessary to amend Section
40 of the California Masonic Code. (Article VI, Voting and Representation; Section 40, Grand Officers)
An appropriate resolution would be as follows :
RESOLVED. that Section 40 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by substituting for the present Section 40 the following :
The Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior Grand
Warden and the Junior Grand Warden shall be entitled to one vote
each. No other Grand Lodge Officer shall be entitled to vote except as
provided in Section 41 of this Code. Past Grand Masters of the Grand
Lodge shall, collectively, be entitled to one vote.
We move the adoption of the resolution.
A majority voted against the resolution.

restaurants, clubs, picnic grounds and similar locations, and as to whether or not Masonic groups may follow the usual and generally accepted
social customs at such aflairs; and

of such gathuings in the normal American way and there will be presented to this Grand Lodge at its 1968 Communication a statement by
the Grand Master that Masons cannot use liquor at a ny dinner dance
or other social gathering which they "attend in a public hotel or other
public place, which is the same as the Prohibition Amendment of the
1920's which proved to be unworkable and unenforceable and therefore
was repealed by the American people;

"Section 324.2. Serving of liquor at social functions. A Masonic
Lodge, or an organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is th.at
a person be a Master Mason, may hold social gatherings, dinners, dinner
dances, picnics and other meetings of a social nature or other social
events at which liquor, wine or beer may be used or served, in a hotel,
restaurant. dining room, club. convention hall. picnic area or other establishment; provided, however. that, except for ritualistic purposes, no

Masonic Lodge or Masonic-relate d organization to vacate leased premises prior to expiration of leases made in good faith, or to violate ]eases,
or to refuse to accept buildings so received from an estate or by gift;
but such building so received must be sold or otherwise disposed of, or
the offending use must be terminated, within a reasonable time."
In our opinion the adoption of the foregoing proposal will eliminate
any aura of uncertainty or hypocrisy about the propriety of serving
alcoholic beverages at purely social functions held outside of Masonic
premises.

above indicated; that if it is so amended. the resolution be adopted; and
in that case the Committee recommends a "yes" vote upon the resolution
as amended.

FORMAL PRESENTATION OF AMERICAN FLAG
AND WHEN DISPLAYED
(7)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A M. of California:
WHEREAS, never has there been a time in the history of this great
nation when the need was so urgent for us all, as true Americans, to
rededicate ourselves to the. principles of freedom upon which our country was founded; and to this end, we should most proudly pledge our
allegiance to our country and its flag at every opporunity, and
WHEREAS, in the Entered Apprentice Degree, we are enjoined to
be exemplary in the discharge of our civil duties; to pay due obedience
to the laws under whose protection we live, and to never lose sight of
the allegiance due to our country, and
WHEREAS, it is the feeling of many that this allegiance can, and
should be, reaffirmed at each meeting of our Lodge by formally presenting the flag of our country at the altar:
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Sections 329-A
and 554-W of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as
follows:
The flag of our country shall be formally presented at the altar a t
all communications of Grand Lodge and carried on all ceremonial occasions except at funerals. At all meetings of our Lodges , the flag shall be
formally presented at the altar by the Marshal and received in the manner prescribed by the Grand Lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM P. DEN NY, M..

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes. and on Ritual.

The Committee on Ritual:
Similar resolutions regarding the formal presentation of the flag
have been presented on numerous occasions before and have been rejected.
The Committee on Ritual has always felt that each Master should
govern his Lodge within the limits set forth in our law, which permits
him to formally present the flag at any meeting he desires. We feel that
the present permissive rule is in the best interest of Masonry.

250

251

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

This Committee feels that the flag of our country should be honored
and Masters are encouraged to do so. Even when the flag is not formally
presented many Masters do and are encouraged to lead their members
in the Pledge of Allegiance upon opening the Lodge.
We move the adoption of the resolution but urge a "no" vote.

and formal presentation must be made at the annual election and at
such other meetings as the Master deems desirable. We therefore feel
the Resolution of 1927 adequately covers all reasonable requirements
for display and presentation of the flag.
However, in order to effect the purpose of the authors of the ·resolution, we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED. that a new section be added to the C.M.C., to be
numbered Section 329.1 , to read as follows :
"The flag of our .countr y shall be formally presented at the altar at
all communications of Grand Lodge and caxried on all ceremonial occasions except at funerals. At all meetings of Lodges, the -flag shall be
formally presented at the altar and received in the manner prescribed
by the Grand Lecturer."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Sections 329a and 554w
C.M.C. be repealed and deleted from the Code, and that the resolution
adopted by Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication in 1927, and
appearing in the Proceedings of 1927 at page 473, be repealed, and that
the provisions of the new Section 329.1 C.M.C. be made a part of the
Monitor in lieu of the resolution adopted in 1927.
We recommend a "no" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred to
it Resolution No. 7 entitled "Formal Presentation of American Flag
and When Displayed."
The preamble to this proposition recites quite properly the necessity
of all Americans and Masons in particular to rededicate themselves to
the "principles of freedom upon which our country was founded ." With
this we thoroughly agree.
The resolution itself calls for the formal presentation of the flag at
the altar at all communications of the Grand Lodge and to be carried
on all ceremonial occasions. It further calls for the formal presenation
of the flag at the altar at all meetings of all Lodges.
The formal presentation of the flag is already a part of the formal
opening of Grand Lodge. At all other ceremonial occasions the flag is
always in evidence if not actually carried in a procession such as might
precede a cornerstone laying .
The constituent Lodges have a ritual for the presentation of the flag
at the opening of the Lodge which is optional. This resolution would
make it compulsory at every opening of the Lodge.
We feel that there are many occasions when this practice should be
followed but we can envision many times when it would be impractical
and unimpressive. For example, many Lodges are opened at an early
hour with a minimum of members present in order to expedite a long
meeting, which is most commendatory.
Your Committee always hesitates to compel the Lodges to do something they are permitted to do on a voluntary basis. We feel that it is
far better for the individual Lodges to determine the proper times for the
presentation of the flag than to force the ceremony on every meeting.
when it might become an habitual and meaningless act.
While in full sympathy with the patriotic spirit which prompted the
proponents of this proposition, we move the adoption of the resolution
but urge a "no" vote.
The Committee on furisprudence:
Resolution No. 7 proposes an amendment to Sections 329a and
554w of the California Masonic Code. These two annotations state
the essence of the resolution adopted by Grand Lodge in 1927 as to the
display of the flag of our country. The presentation of the flag at all
communications of Grand Lodge is already a part of the Grand Lodge
ritual. As to Lodges, the flag is required to be displayed at all meetings

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes :
Resolution No. 12, as presented, proposes to amend our law to provide discretionary power by a Master or Warden, in the matter of the
burial with Masonic Honors of Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft
Masons.
Your Committee has carefully considered a number of arguments
presented on this resolution and is fully in accord with the interest and
purposes of the proponents of this resolution and we firmly believe that
every Mason in good standing should be entitled to this. the last public
act of our recognition and esteem which we can extend to one whom we
have accepted into our Fraternity and whom we have ·c alled 'Brother.'
We feel nothing is or can be gained by or for our Fraternity by denying this privilege to a bereaved widow or family of a deceased Brother
Mason while a great deal of harm and disillusionment can actually
result from such denial.
We do not. however, believe that this should be made a 'discretionary' matter, as proposed in the original resolution but that the sole test
of eligibility for such consideration should be whether or not the Brother
is in 'good standing.'
The Committee on Jurisprudence will propose language which will
establish the policy which we are recommending to you and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote on the
legislation which that Committee will present.

The Committee on Policy and Genera/ Purposes:
Resolution No. 14 proposes to amend Section 493-2nd to require
that only one annual statement of income and expenditures, assets and
liabilities be presented to the Lodge.
Your Committee has given careful consideration to the reasons
advanced by the proponents of this resolution, especially to the fact that
in some cases the mid-year report 'unrealistically' reflects the income
portion of the report when compared with the year-end report, however.
the income and expenditure portions of the required statements are only
a small portion of the total report.
The essential portion of these reports actually lies in the Asset and
Liability portions and, if these portions are properly and accurately completed the 'unrealism' referred to in the resolution will automatically
disappear.
We are of the opinion that the brethren of the lodge are entitled to
an accurate and factual presentation of the flnancial status of their lodge
at least twice a year: once so that it may be determined if finance-wise
the lodge is currently living within its means and that anticipated income
is being met and projected expenditures are not being exceeded and
secondly so that the year to year revenue and expenditure projections
will remain realistic.
We are authorized by the Committee on Jurisprudence to state that
the language proposed. if adopted, will accomplish the intended purpose
of the proponents.
We therefore move the adoption of the resolution but strongly urge
a "no" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Ritual. to which was referred Resolution No. 15,
proposing that physical qualifications "would be conformed to if the
candidate wore a modern, improved hearing aid while taking the degrees
of Masonry" has carefully considered the proposal and makes the following observations and recommendation:
Your C ommittee on R itual objects to this proposed relaxation of our
physical qualification requ irements as set forth in Sections 511 and 512,
C.M.C. Our objections are based on our expressed and stated position
set forth in our report and recommenda tions made and presented on
Resolution No. 18, which has to do with " physical qualifications."
Resolution No. 15 would single out one particular form of disability
as being acceptable in a candidate-hearing -; its acceptability over
other forms of disabilities requiring 'aids' being based, in our opinion,
merely on a matter of degree.
An identical resolution was presented at our 1966 Annual Comm unication, and received a simple majority vote. The matter was again voted
on as a 'hold-over' at our 1967 Communica tion, and was rejected overwhelmingly.
Again, we reiterate that this Grand Lodge's position on physical
qualification should not be changed without some change in the condition of the Craft which would compel it. We may properly inquire if a
change has occurred in the condition of the Craft which would now
require a change in our ancient regulation. We know of none.
We unequivocably disapprove this resolution . and strongly urge a
"no" vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution would remove the disqualification for our degrees
which attaches to an applicant who must rely upon the use of a hearing
aid; that disqualification was declared by the Grand Master and approved by Grand Lodge in 1949.
While during the intervening nineteen years science and a rt have
d eveloped hearing aids which are almost undiscernible from the exterior,
your Committee prefers to base our approval of this resolution upon our
opinion that the corrective device would in no way ha ndicap a candidate
in conforming to the ritual of our degrees. It is difficult for us to understand any substantial difference between an applicant who must wear a
hearing aid and one who must rely upon strong corrective glasses.
As indicated in the preliminary recitals of this resolution, this disqualification does not exist in a number of other Masonic jurisdictions,
and we know of no resulting detriment in their experience. We believe
that the time has come to eliminate the restriction in our jurisdiction.

arduous and hazardous, and a physically impaired workman constituted
a danger to himself and his fellow workers, and liable to become a
burden to his Lodge or Guild. and

have expressed a desire to a pply for the degrees of Masonry, but have
been denied because of having been wounded, maimed. or otherwise
physically disabled in the defense of our country, or by other misfortune or tragedy. and now find it necessary to employ the aid of a
prostheses to perform their daily tasks to the livelihood . comfort. safety,
or necessity of the individual who should not be denied the privilege of
receiving the degrees of M asonry so long as he can substantially con~
form to the ritual, and
WHEREAS, it is well known that many members of our Craft have
befallen such misfortune after taking the degrees and are thereby unable

written or unwritten laws,

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes. and on Ritual.
The Committee on Ritual, to which was referred Resolution No. 18
proposing the elimination of the requirements of physical qualifications
or modification of our existing requirements, has carefully considered the
proposal. We have considered it without emotion and only from the
standpoint of what in our opinion would be good for Masonry.
Masonry selects its candidates and admits them only after careful
investigation and a unanimous ballot. No one has a right to become a
Mason. It is a privilege granted to a comparatively small number.
To begin with, we exclude half of the human race. No woman can
become a Mason. Half of the remainder of the population is likewise
excluded, namely anyone under the required age of 21 years. In Califor-

nia, for more than one hundred years, we have adhered to the regulation
that no one having a maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable of learning the art and physically unable to conform to what the
several degrees respectively require of him, can become a Mason.

266

267

The physical requirements for qualification of candidates for the
degr.ees of Mason~y are probably as old as Masonry itself. They are a
survival of OperatJVe Masonry and are peculiar to the Masonic institution, just as are the regulations excluding women and minors. One of the
Ancient Landmarks stated by Dr. Mackey, and which for several
.decad~.s has been printed in the Ross Digest and our Masonic Code.
is the qualification of candidates for initiation ," as the 18th Landmark.
A natural sympathy for those unfortunate men who have suffered
severe physical injuries has caused numerous proposals to change the
old requirements, and these have been presented throughout the history
of our Grand Lodge, most recently in 1961-1962. 1963, 1964, 1966-1967.
They have been rejected except for the compromise which resulted in
the adoption of our present regulations many years ago, now contained
in Sections 511 and 512 of the C.M.C.: "having no maim or defe·c t in
his body that may render him incapable of learning the art, and physic~lly able t? confo~m .~ubstantially. to what the several degrees respectively require of him. The question as to physical sufficiency of the
applicant is left to the sound discretion of the Lodge, and it is determined
by the ritual.
. . Since the rule as to physical qualification has existed for so long that
it is at least regarqed as one of the Ancient Landmarks it should not be
changed without some change in the condition of the Craft which would
compel it. We may properly inquire what change has occurred in the
condition of the Craft which would now require a change in our ancient
regulation, We know of none. Masonry does not go out and seek candidates; we select those who apply, and they must apply of their own free
will and accord.
If these proposals were adopted , it would require a different ritual
for each case of physical defect, depending upon the nature and severity
of the particular deformity. This would completely destroy any uniformity in the ritual. Under our law, the conferring of a degree must be
in conformity with the established ritual taught by the Grand Lecturer.
and the conferring of a degree in a merely symbolic manner is out of the
question. (CMC Section 512-j.) Unless we are prepared to do away
with uniformity of the ritual. carefully built up for a century, and prescribed by Sections 551 and 555 of the CMC. we cannot change the
rule as to physical qualifications. This proposed legislation does not purport to change Sections 551 or 555 of the Code.
In our opinion, this Grand Lodge has alrea dy gone as far in meeting

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes amendment of Sections 511 and 512 of the
California Masonic Code to provide for admission of applicants for
degrees who have suffered loss of limb or limbs or other impairment
which can be remedied with the aid of a prosthesis, thereby rendering
them capable of learning the art and physically able to conform substantially to the requirement s of the several degrees ..
This resolution presents a direct confrontatio n between the requirements of traditional regulations and fundamenta l Masonic principles. In
balance and stark contrast stand the tenet of Brotherly love and the
requirement s of present Masonic law.
The fact that 011r present rule has existed for a long period of time
establishes no case for its merit. Rather, the fact that almost no Mason
feels entirely comfortable with this regulation , makes timely and thorough examination of its merits highly desirable.
All men are captives of their corporeal beings. and stand in constant
risk of debilitating and humiliating injury. Accident and unfortunate
happenstanc e cast a dark enough shadow across the lives of us all. No
man or group of men should add to this burden without having serious
and compelling reasons so to do.
That our rules as they now stand add to the already frightful burden
of the maimed and injured is beyond question. With the rejected applicant. the effect is direct and immediate. But all men embraced within
the ambit of our rules are poorer as a result. Only the strongest reasons
should cause us to add the weight of disqualification to all of the uncertainties and self-doubts associated with serious injury.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that such
compelling reasons do not exist. With the aid of modern prosthetic
science, seriously injured persons can perform tasks that require great
agility and dexterity. Many men who have suffered the loss of a limb or
limbs, or other physical injury. can substantiall y (and in some cases
fully) comply with the requirement s of our degrees. These men in our
opinion should be able to participate in our privileges.
These new applicants would doubtless benefit from a Masonic affiliation. Our Lodges would have a new source of interest and strength.
Most importantly. we would stand taller as men and Masons by so providing.
Your Committee moves the adoption of Resolution No. 18 and
recommends an affirmative vote.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 546 of the C.M.C. in essence provides that "if a candidate
does not present himself properly qualified for the Second and Third
Degrees within a period of five years from the date of his initiation as
an Entered Apprentice." two things shall occur. The first is that "the
Master shall direct the Secretary to forward to such candidate, by registered mail to his last known address, a notice advising him that unless
he shall present himself for advancement on or before a specified date
(at least sixty days in advance) his fees for the unconferred degrees
and all of his previous contributions will be declared forfeited." The
second thing which occurs-after the registered mail notice and the
minimum sixty day grace period-is that "on the day specified, the
Master shall declare the fees forfeited."
Resolution No. 20, citing 534 such forfeitures during fiscal 19661967, and estimating an annual forfeiture rate of 516 by the year 1972,
asserts that unless the requirements of Section 546 C.M.C. are published in the Application Form, the "Information to Candidates" booklet, and added to the instructions of Investigating Committees and
Coaches, these requirements to complete the three degrees within five
years "may therefore be overlooked in the consequent dependence upon
word-of-mouth transmittal of information to the Candidate."
First. it might be noted that current statistics from the office of the
Grand Secretary show a sharp decrease in such forfeitures-the number
having decreased from 534 last year to 318 for fiscal 1967-1968.
Second, there is no valid basis whatever upon which it can be asserted
that any or all of these forfeitures occurred because the candidates involved did not know that there was a requirement that they complete
their degrees within five years.
On the contrary, the mandatory provisions of 546 C.M.C.-which

GllAND LODGE OF CAUPORN!A

273

prevent any forfeiture until and unless direct written notice by registered
mail to the candidate concerned be given, coupled with an extens ion of
at least sixty days beyond the five year period, in which the candidate
may still be able to avoid forfeiture, leave the probability that other
causes of dissatisfaction have alienated the candidate's interest.
Certainly nothing supports the real basis for Resolution No. 20--that the requirement to complete degrees within five years. and the candidate's knowledge of that fact , involves "dependence upon word-ofmouth transmittal of information to the candidate."
In the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes,
the requirement that degrees be completed within five years is wholly
reasonable, and the existing Section 546 guarantees that no forfeitures
will occur without prior written notice to the candidate involved.
Accordingly, the Committee moves the adoption of Resolution No.
20 and urges a "no" vote thereon.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This Resolution proposes that the Grand Lodge Form No. 235 .
which is the form for applying for the Degrees, be revised to include
the pertinent provisions of Section 546 C.M.C. relating to the forfeiture
of the fees and contributions of Candidates who do not complete the
work of the Three Degrees within a five year period and the "In formation to Candidates" booklet and the instructions to coaches in the
"Coaches Handbook" be revised to include this information.
Your committee does not feel that it is necessary to amend any Sections of the California Masonic Code to accomplish the purpose of
the proposers of this Resolution since all references are to forms and
booklets published by this Grand Lodge. We accordingly present the
following:
RESOLVED, that there be added to the Grand Lodge Application
Form No. 235 a footnote reading substantially as follows:
"Please be advised that if a candidate does not present himself.
properly qualified, for the Second and Third Degrees within a period
of five years from the date he is initiated as an Entered Apprentice, then
his fees for the Degrees which have not been conferred and his contributions will be forfeited."
FURTHER RESOLVED; that similar language be included in the
"Information to Candidates" booklet and in the instructions to coaches
in the "Coaches Handbook" published by this Grand Lodge.
A majority voted against the resolution.

(21)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 0 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. the Grand Lodge of California requires as a part of
Section 527 of the C.M.C. (Form of Application for Degrees) under
Question No. 15 the following:
" Do you promise that you will not apply for or receive any degree
or be initiated in any Lodge, Order or organization the prerequisite of
membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason, until you have
given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge, that
you are entirely proficient and well qualified in the Candidate's Lecture
of the Degree of Master Mason and in no event within twelve months
after you have received the Degree of Master Mason?" and
WHEREAS. the portion which reads, "and in no event within twelve
months after you have received the Degree of Master Mason," was
designed for the purpose of retaining the newly raised brother's interest
and attendance in his Blue Lodge, and
WHEREAS. it has not accomplished its purpose but has in fact
allowed a period of Masonic inactivity during which time our Brethren
have turned to other interests and grown further away from their Masonic involvement, and
WHEREAS, it is believed that voluntary activity promoted by an
attractive program as well as the cooperation of all Masonic bodies one
with another will better serve our Masonic purpose,
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 527 be amended
to delete from Question No. 15 the words "and in no event within
twelve months after you have received the Degree of Master Mason?"
and shall hereafter read:
Do you promise that you will not apply for or receive any degree
or be initiated in any Lodge, Order or organization the prerequisite of
membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason, until you
have given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge,
that you are entirely proficient and well-qualified in the Candidate's
Lecture of Master Mason?
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED. that all other references contained in our laws, rules, regulations. edicts, decisions, or any other
matter on this subject, written or unwritten, having the force of law,
which are contrary hereto are rescinded.
Respectfully submitted,
Roy V. ANDERSON, P.M. , No. 20

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 21 proposes to amend that part of Section 527 of the
C.M.C. by dispensing with the requirement that an applicant for degrees
promise that he will not petition for or accept membership in any of
the so-<:alled affiliated organizations until twelve months after he has
received his Third Degree.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees with the
proponents of this resolution that the twelve month prohibition against
affiliation has not accomplished its intended purpose--that of retaining
a newly obligated Brother's interest and attendance in his Lodge. To
the contrary, it is now a widely held view that this prohibition has had
the effect of "cooling off" a Brother's interest in Masonry. thus losing
him to other involvements not Masonically connected.
The fear that affiliation with the Scottish Rite, York Rite, the Shrine,
et al., will preempt a Brother's time to devote to his Blue Lodge has
little or no foundation. This is demonstrated by the large number of
us who have many Mason ic affiliations but yet are active in the affairs
of our own Blue Lodge. This is to say nothing of the many actively participating Blue Lodge members who became active only after the flame
was kindled by activity in an affiliated body. When the reasoning upon
which an ordinance is predicated is demonstrated to be false, then the
ordinance should be repealed.
Your Committee points to the fact that this resolution does not affect
the requirement that a Master Mason must demonstrate his proficiency
in the candidates' lecture of the Third Degree before he may join other
prerequisite bodies. Your Committee expressly disapproves any attempt
to eliminate the proficiency requirement as will be reflected by the nex t
report.
We move the adoption of Resolution No. 21 and recommend a
"yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
After receiving the degree of Maste.r Mason, a Brother is now required not only to give evidence of his proficiency in the candidate lecture of that degree but also to wait a period of twelve months before
joining organizations in which being a Master Mason is a prerequisite.
This resolution would eliminate the twelve month waiting period.
This resolution requires amendment of Section 527 of the California
Masonic Code and the deletion of certain of the annotations in that
section.
Effect would be given to the intent of the proponents of the resolution if the following were adopted:
"RESOLVED. that Section 527 of the California Masonic Code

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 24 recommending the refund of dues paid in advance
when a member dimits has been referred to your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes and after a careful study we report as follows:
The title of this resolution could be misleading as it refers to "Refund
due paid in advance on affiliation." Actually the resolution proposes to
refund dues paid in advance when a member <limits, which is quite
another thing.
When a Brother is issued a <limit, that document keeps him in good
standing as a Mason at large for a period of one year. This privilege
should certainly be worth any dues paid in advance.
It is true that the wording of the resolution states "when a member
dimits to affiliate with another lodge." After a dimit is issued, however,
there is no assurance that the brother will ever affiliate and therefore
he could enjoy the benefits and privileges of Masonry for a period of
a year, after receiving a refund of any advance dues paid. We feel that
the advantage of remaining in good standing is well worth the small
sacrifice of any dues paid in advance.
To put the proposition before Grand Lodge therefore I move the
adoption of the resolution but your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes recommends a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The purpose of the proposed resolution is to refund dues paid in
advance, if requested by a member of the Lodge seeking to dimit to another Lodge.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence thinks that the language of the
original resolution should be amended as follows:
RESOLVED: A third paragraph shall be added to Section 557
(1st) of the California Masonic Code as follows:
"Lodges within this jurisdiction shall refund to a Brother on his
request dues paid in advance of the current quarter when he dimits to
affiliate with another Lodge."
We move the adoption of the resolution without recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

BOARDS OF RELIEF-WHO REPRESENT LODGE
(26)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Maste·r and Wardens of a lodge are a Charity
Committee of that lodge (Section 360. CMC) and are usually men of
the highest calibre, reflecting the best judgment and confldence of the
brethren of the lodge, and
WHEREAS. to relieve the distressed is one of the most important
functions of a lodge, and not to be handled perfunctorily, nor to be considered lightly, and
WHEREAS, the present method of appointing or electing of lodge
representatives to a Board of Relief, is often made on the basis of who is
willing, rather than who is best qualified, and
WHEREAS, longevity of representatives beyond two or three years
is not always in the best interests of Masonry, and
WHEREAS, it is desirous that Boards of Relief be composed of

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes to add to Section 603 C.M.C. the provision that the representative of the several lodges comprising a Board
of Relief shall consist of the Master and Wardens, and that the Master
may not delegate his or the Wardens' authority to represent the lodge.
The imposition Of such a restriction upon the Master is required by
the proponents on the assumption that it is not desirable for a representative of a lodge to serve on a Board of Relief longer than three
years. Whether or not this assumption is true, we do not choose to
debate. Rather, your committee is concerned with another effect of the
resolution.
In properly administering the alfairs of the Lodge, the Master should
have the discretion of selecting the representa tives to the board. What
may be best for one lodge will not necessarily be good for others. The
control of Lodge business should be flexible to suit the particular situation.
The second provision in this resolution would permit the ranking
representative present. in the absence of either or both other representatives, to cas t a vote in behalf of the absent member or members.
Your committee takes no position on this part of the resolution.
We are authorized to report that the Committee on furis prudence
has found the text of the resolution will accomplish its intended purpose.
A s presented, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
moves the adoption of Resolution No. 26 and recommends a "no" vote.
A majority vo ted against the resolution.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California;

America, is at present inadequately displayed at the exterior of the Memorial Temple, now
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED : That the flag of our beloved
country be appropriately and prominently displayed daily from a staff
a t the front of the Memorial Temple or on the roof thereof, so that it

283

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple.

The Board of Truste.es of California Masonic Memorial Temple has
studied carefully Resolution No. 28 requiring that the flag of our country
be displayed daily from a staff at the front of the Temple, or on the
roof thereof, so that it may be seen in full view from a distance of not
less than two city blocks by persons approaching the Temple from either
direction on California Street. A similar resolution was defeated by
Grand Lodge at the 1966 communication after a "no" vote was ·r ecommended by the Finance Committee and the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes.
The Board of Trustees of the Temple desires to make the following
observations:
l. At the prese~t ti~e the flag of our country is prominently displayed at the entrance of the Temple immediately over the main entrance
door. In addition, the flag of our country is displayed daily on a staff
on the Taylor Street side of the Temple along with the flags of the States
of California and Hawaii. The three staffs are 15 feet apart to allow
adequate space for the flags to be separately flown. A visit to the site
where the flags are displayed will show that they are visible to a very
large part of the City to the east. including a view from such prominent
edifices as the Equitable Life Building, Wells Fargo Building, Sir Francis Drake Hotel. Clift Hotel and many other buildings.
2. It would be almost physically impossible for the flags to be raised
and lowered from the roof of the Temple. Without substantial structural
changes, there would be no way for the staffs to be reached each day
for raising and lowering the flags. Also, if the flags were displayed on
the roof they would not be seen for two full city blocks by persons approaching the Temple from either direction on California Street. As a
matter of fact, if the flags were displayed on the roof of the Temple
they would be seen by far ff!'Ner persons than can see the flags where
they are presently displayed.

285

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRl\ND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

3. There is no place on the California Street side of the Temple
where the flags could be displayed so as to be seen from a distance of
two city blocks. Persons approaching the Temple from the west could
not possibly see such flags until they reached the intersection of California and Jones Streets. In addition, there is talk of a high rise building
being erected immediately to the west of the Temple and a full view
of the flags from the west could be cut off.
It would not be possible for persons approaching the Temple from
the east to see the flags for a distance of two city blocks. The hill on
California Street between Powell and Mason Streets would prevent
such an extended view.
The Board of Trustees admires the spirit of those who propose the
resolution, but feel that the terms of the resolution could not be complied with and feel that the national emblem is at present adequately
displayed both in the interior and exterior of the Temple and that architecturally and practically it would not be feas ible to change the location
of the staffs flying the flags of our country and states of our jurisdiction.
Your Board of Trustees therefore unanimously recommends a " no"
vote on the resolution.

Ref erred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes, and to the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 29 would require, if desired by the donor or donors,
that contributions made to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund be
credited to a lodge or lodges of their choice and selection .
It has become a common practice for the family of a deceased Brother to ask that Endowment contributions be made in lieu of flowers.
Through this custom free-will contributions are made by many family
friends who may have no connection with the Fraternity. To ask that
these persons designate a particular lodge or lodges in order to swell
the credited contributions of the members of the lodge goes far beyond
the limits of Masonic propriety.
The contributions credited to the lodges by the Masonic Homes Endowment Board are a measure of the concern in each lodge for the care
of our brethren, their widows and orphans. We do not ask non-members
to contribute in our annual Endowment effort nor do we think we should
start now.
In order to bring the resolution before the Grand Lodge we move the
adoption of Resolution No. 29 and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "no" vote.
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board indicated its concurrence in the
recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.
